LADY MEDICAL OFFICEDS.

13y twelve votcs to Eve the guardians of _St. Gecrge's, Hanover-square, have declined to allow lady practitioners to compete for the post of second assistant medical ofncer to the workhouse. The reason given is interesting, if illogical. "A lady would be sure to wrangle with the male doctors." I am not prepared, remarks a writer in the Lady, to assert that women make as good doctors as men. but as men have themselves opened the medical profession 'to women, they might at least not try to arrest their progress in it ty airing such "old wives' " prejuaices as this which I have quoted. If there is no differenee of opinion among male doctors in institutions like the workhouse, so much the worse for those insthutions; as where all is peace all is seldom right. If a lady doctor is less easily induced to hold her tongue than a man, she is a greater ornament to her profession than I had imagined. _
CHAPTER XXII.
THE SCOURGE.

Fr was not fill three months after the dis- appearance of William Jordison .and his servants that the first clue of their existence came to light. It came, much to the disgust of those who pinned their faith to Sherlock Holmes, to the despised police at Warley Dalc in Yorkshire.

A daring burglary had been committed at the country house of a wealthy steel manu- facturer. Jewels, valued at izo,ooo, had been stolen, and the thieves had made ofl without interruption. The loss was not discovered until the next morning. Mr. Strangways, doubtful of the ability of the local police, wired for a detective from Scot- land Yard, but before the man arrived, a stolid Yorkshire constable made a discovery of the greatest importance. He was searching the lawns and drive for footprints, but there had been a heavy rain the night before, and he found no trace of any kind whatever, except the fresh tracks of the people who had passed_ up the drive in the morning. Then, as he was walking through some dead and rotting leaves that the wind had gathered into a small ridge by the edge of the path; his foot struck something hard. Stooping down, he picked up a small steel spanner. It was greasy to the touch and smelt strongly of oil. He examined it care- fully, and found that it was made by the firm of Jacquart et Cie in Paris. The name con- veyed nothing to his mind, but his slow brain grasped the ?act that it was a possible clue to the discovery of the binglars. He had a dim idea that it might be part of their equipment for breaking open the safe. He said nothing to his colleague, but when the detective arrived from London he showed him the spanner and asked his opinion. Kennedy, a big, keen-eyed, quiet man, turned it over and over in his hand and smelt it cared fully. Then be looked at the name stamped on its surface, and a smile of triumph came over his face. He already saw himself the possessor of a comfortable income for life, and the little country cottage where he hoped to spend the rest of his days, seemed quite near to him.

"Say nothing of this to anyone," he said, after a pause. "It is absolutely necessary that this discovery should not get into the newspapers." "What is it?" agked the constable. "It is a spanner for a motor and was made in France. Do these facts bring anything to your. mind ? "_

A motor ? " said the policeuran slowly. "Mi. Strangways has a motor." " A steel manufacturer is hardly, ,i"zely to get his spanners from France. Besides, the name is quite sufficient clue to the• thieves of last night." The constable shook his head. These London detectives were beyond him. He had read of them in books, and knew that they arrived at wonderful conclusions: Still, he felt proud to be talking to so clever a man, and tried to look intelligent. "Do you remember the murder of Lord Overcliffe ? " the detective continued, "and the story of William Jordison ? " . The man's face brightened. He slowly grasped the situation. The reference to the motor became cleat to him.

" PO,OOO I" was all that he could gasp out. "Yes," Kennedy replied, " and half of it is yours, if you keep your mouth shut. If you don't, neither of us vill touch a penny. The clue is a certain one. Jordison used to be chairman of Jacquart et Cie. It only remains for us to follow the clue up. This is a great, mark you, a great discovery. But keep your mouth shut. Are you married ? '
" Yes, sir." "Well, don't tell your wife anything. Now let's have another look room!,"

The reappearance of the celebrated black motor car would have provided many columns for the newspapers, but not a word of the discovery reached them. The robbery at- tracted but little attention in the London dailies. The police, said the "Daily Telegraph," had a clue, and were following it up. In less than a week the whole affair was forgotten: Had it occurred two months earlier half Eng- land would have attributed it to Jordison and his servants, and thousands would have rushed to the spot in hope of ferreting out some clue. But now it fell flat on a nation that was exhausting all its energies on the Fiscal question. Only Kennedy and the silent stolid policeman of Warley Dale knew the truth. The one quietly followed up the clue that chance had given him. The other went his daily rounds and kept his mouth shut. But before another fortnight had passed, the Duke of Barstowe's castle in Sornersetshire was broken into. A footman was strangled to death, and the famous Barstowe Tiara was stolen. No, trace was found of the thieves, but Kennedy took up the broken thread of his clue again and started on a fresh trail.

pocket. That very evening posters narea out all over London with "Authentic News of Jordison," and the first real evidence against this determined criminal appeared in print. The clamour increased, .and the result was quite as the shrewd detective had imagined. The robberies ceased and the thieves retired into their hiding-place. . Arthur Holme nad taken no part whatever in the general search for William Jordison. For reasons which were known only to him- self he had no desire to ever meet the man again. He knew, however, ,that Jorclison was more than anxious :to get information from him, and he, wondered why no attempt had been made to' recapture him. Day and night he had a loaded revolver ready to his hand, for this was the only answer he was prepared to give to any of Jordison's ques- tions. But he was unmolested, and finally came to the conclusion-that the man was dead, and that it was the body of the master which had been found in the charred ruins of the stables, and not that of one of his servants.

But, in any case, Holme had been too .busy to play the part of an amateur detective. The commission on the oyster fisheries had occupied four months, and had been. brought to a satisfactory conclusion. The infected oysters had been traced to three pans in one village. The creeks had, been declared free of sewage, and rigorous methods had been instituted by which all danger of future, con- tamination would be avoided. This result, which remit like the work of a week, was not aceomplished without infinite tact and labour. Holme came out of the. ordeal with credit. Be perfiffraed tut duties with firmness and delicacy,. ancl laid 'a restrain- ing hand on all the partit; concerned. If the doctors and scientists had heen left to their own devices, the fishermen would have thrown' them into the water to juin the oysters. But it was Holme, who conciliated the furious and starving men, and showed. theoi how out of much evil might conie e,ue(l. Fur a while they obeyed, but, looked on him with sus- picion. But when they. found that the end had justified the means, and that the report of the commission had chaired tire, distriet of an undeserved • opprohriura , they hailed Hohne as their deliverer. and raced him on a pedestal that was nearly as high as that of their patron Saint ,Nicliclas.

With all this work in hand, and with the prospect ot an election looming in the near future, it can well be . imagined that Arthur Holme had no time to.. spare for detective work. Yet ,he had read' tile papers carefully and knew as much cf hhe .mysterious thieves as most men. He had watched with a smile the heat of the first onthusiasm, and the mar- vellous rapidity with 'Which it had :died away.. He had noted the long: list of burglaries, and read with approval the article which stirred up the dead embers into a blazing :furnace. He only wondered why Essex', the source of the whole category of crimes, had no story to add to the fund of general information. . Then one March evening news was brought to him which- sent- him poet- haste • to -Heather-. stone Hall, and converted- the case of William Jordison frOrn-an abstea4 prohlem into a per- . , • • sonal matter.

The black motor car'had been seen for the first time since the destruction of the. House, and not only had it been seen, but it had been seed in Essex.. And that very same day Lady Agiies -Chile had gone out for a walk in the park, and had nevcr returned to Heather Stone

The very next week, the safe of the Welsh National Bank of Bangor was blown open with dynamite, and several hundred pounds in gold were taken. Again the thieves got. clear with their 'booty, and again Kennedy took up the fresh soent. During the next month another bank was broken into, and there were five great jewel robberies in different parts of England and Scotland. One of them took place in Inver- ness, and another in Sussex, within twenty- four hours of each other, so that it was clear if the two were the work of the same gang oi thieves, that they had at their command very rapid means of transit. In all thesa instances the criminals got clear away wite their spoil, and left no clue behind them. It was then that the Crime Investigator of a halfpenny morning paper wrote a special article for his journal. The article iva.s headed, " Has Jordison come to Life &pin ? " and it set forth a reasonable theory taat all these robberies were the work of one gang of thieves, and that in all probability Jordisoii and his accomplices were responsible for the bulk of them. The indefatigable writer had traced and catalogued a score of smaller robberies, which had hitherto been of purely local interest and had never beea noticed in the London papers—mere thefts of bread and meat and spirits from .shops and farm- houses. He prepared an elaborate plan of dates and places and pointed Out that all the minor thefts had occurred on probable lines ot route between two successive jewel robberies, and that the dates were consistent with the theory that these small affairs were merely the means of getting food, while journeying from one job to another. The next (lay toe paper published a map dotted with dates and places, and made the theory plain to the meanest intelligence. Detective Kennedy ground his teeth, and swore an assortment of fancy oaths, as he read this article, and he - tyre the map into fifty pieces before he put it 0.1, he fire. The same idea had occurred to ii!t, and in his pocket was a piece of paper with a similar list of dates and places. His own was perhaps a trifle more complete', and included one of vital and peculiar importance, namely, the theft of a few gallons of petrol from a bicycle shop, but substantially the two were the same. Ken- nedy cursed the clever fool who had thrown all this information to the public, like pearls before swine. Naturally secretive and silent, he did not understand the true spirit of journalism, which is to shout out all you know as los.dly as possible. Before a week was over all England fell at the feet of the Crime Investigator and hailed him as a leader of men. The amateur detec- tives emerged from their obscurity- and once more the drivers of big cars suffered untold annoyance. The hue and cry was raised all over England. The seekers after the £lo.oos reward were perhaps a trifle more cautious than they had been in the first instance, but they proved themselves an intolerable nuisance to all peaceable citizens. Kennedy saw that the, game was up, and that the results of his own patient researches 0 in the bands of every fool in the United Kingdom. He resolved to make what he could out of his information. One morning he called at the offices of a great evening paper and left there with a Slll,6tdatial ':II.:QtIC in his

pause. "He came down last night to see it he could help us in any way. You will of course, stay the night. We shall be glad of your com- pany, and perhaps between the three of us we may be able to work out some solution of this problem. Ah ! here is Harry himself." Lord Harry Quy came towards them, hesitated a moment, and then shook hands silently with Holme. 'The two young men had not met for several months. A certain coolness had sprung up between them, in spite of their strenuous efforts to resist any feelings of jealousy. Their correspondence had died down to the exchange of an occasional formal letter dealing with political matters. Lord Harry, to whom Lord Heatherstone had un- burdened his soul in the first heat of anger against Arthur Holme, felt that his friend had not acted quite honestly towards him. Holme, who had for a long time fought against the clin.:tates of his own heart out of loyalty to his friend, bitterly resented • the imputation, which, though it had never been expressed in words, had been made manifest by Lord Harry's manner towards him. But all the red passions grow pale in the presence of death, and in the shadow of a common grief all the fierce and angry fires die out from the human heart. The girl they both loved was either dead or else in the hands of a madman, who had hitherto let nothing stand between him and his desires. They were united by a common bond, and resolved to save or avenge her. The bond was sealed in silence by a single clasp of their hands. Its terms were not set forth in words, but it was understood that they worked together with- out regard to what the future held for either of them.

After dinner they sat that evening over the smoking-room fire and thrashed out the whole question of where it would be best to search for William Jordison. Lord Heatherstone admitted that it would be like looking for a needle in a haystack. Lord Harry Quy who had come down from London on a new motor- car of extraordinary power and speed. thought that he would be able to trace Jordi- son to his hiding place, if he could once get fairly started on a warm trail. Holme, whose ideas were local, thought that Jordison was in the neighbourhood, and that the letter posted from Up Withing in •Yorkshire was a mere blind. He could assign, so he said, no other motive for the writing of such a letter. The next morning, after an early breakfast at eight o'clock, Lord Harry Quy took Arthur Holine round to the stables to inspect the new motor-car. It had been manufactured by a well-known firm, and had only just been put 3n the market. It represented the " Last word" of the motor world, in regard to power and speed. It was an eight cylinder oar, 120 i.h.p., and had attained at a recent speed trial the terrific pace of ninety-seven miles an hour. It had cost £4,000. In ap- pearance it was long, low hung, wide, and ugly. It had not yet received its final coat of paint, and was coloured a dull grey, like a modern battleship. The luxurious padded seats of the modern car were conspicuous by their absence, for Lord Harry had not yet decided on the type of body. There were only two seats, and these were little more than a frame work of steel. The general aspect of the machine was that of a human body, stripped of its flesh, and showing only the bones and muscles. - .

Arthur Holme looked at the unsightl) object in silence. He could not pretend tc feel the admiration that Lord Harry Quy ex- pressed in every feature. But he realised that the mere ugliness of the thing spoke well for its serviceable qualities. Evidently no money had been wasted on outward show or decoration.
"She's a beauty, isn't she ? " said Lord Harry, after looking at it for a minute or two in silent admiration.

• " replied Hohne, " how fast do you say ? " ' I shall get one hundred miles an hour out of her when her engines settle down a bit." "Do you think you can beat Jordison's car ? " " I have never seen it, but I- reckon this car could walk round any machine that was ever made. I paid a large premium to get it. The sister car is racing three days from now : against some of the finest cars in the world. The makers are betting even money against i the field."

Holme looked at it critically. He did not know anything about motor-cars. He could have criticised the lines of a yacht, but this ugly grey lump of machinery was outside his sphere of knowledge. He saw, however, that it might be very useful to him in tracking down Jordison, if it represented. all that was claimed for it.

"I tell you what we'll do, Harry," he said after a pause, "if you will consent. We will start in, an hour's time for Up Withing in Yorkshire, and see if we can find any trace of Jordison having been there. Then we will come back here and thoroughly examine the whole of Essex. I am still convinced that Jordison is hiding not far from this very house."
"Where do you think he is; somewhere in the marshes ?

" Yes. It seems ridiculous, doesn't it ? The marshes are better adapted for a yacht than a motor-car. But they would offer an excellent place of concealment. , For the most part they are totally uninhabited and almost inaccessible."

Lord Harry smiled. " You forget the motor," he said, " no motor could possibly be hidden in the marshes for the simple reason that it could not be driven across them. It would have to be concealed somewhere near the road. Every inch of the roads has been searched, and no one has discovered any hiding place that would conceal a large car like rordison's." " You are right, Quy," Holme answered gloomily, "the marshes are out of the ques- 'tion. He must have concealed himself some- where else in Essex."

Or in England," Lord Harry replied. "It is, as Lord Heatherstone said last night, like looking for a needle in a bundle of hay. For my own part I don't think he is in this part of the world at all. It is naturally the last place, he would choose for a hiding place.' " And therefore one that would commend itself to a clever scoundrel," said Hohne. "Do .you remember Poe's story of the 'Pur- loined Letter ? ' It will at any rate be hope- less to search all England." "A good many people are in the hunt," Quy replied ; " io,ooo is a lot of money. I should say that every square mile of the United Kingdom has been searched during the last month or two."

"And yet nothing has,been found. The car has only once been seen and that was on the road at the bottom of the park. The man who Saw it was not sober at the time and may have been mistaken. It seems hopeless." ' "We are bound to hear something," Lord Harry replied, "and if we do we shall be in a position to 'follow it up. I wager that if we once catch sight of Mr. Jordison's car we shall overtake it.' And he looked admiringly at the 120 h.p. monster before him." "When will you be ready to start ? " "In about an hour. We had 'better take a bag with a few things for each of us. There's no knowing when our journey will end." No," answered Holme, "nor what we shall find at the end of it. But I will not rest until Jordison is brought to the gallows." "Nor I," said Lord Harry Quy. .Holme held out his hand, and his friend took it i 4 silence. - At halt-pt ten in the morning the grey car glided dawn the drive and into the open country, and before dark it had reached the little village of Up Withing in Yorkshire,

Mr. A. L, Rotch, the American meteorologist, describes in "Appalachia" his five ascents of Mont Blanc. In the first he was attacked by "mountain sickness," but found some relief on breathing oxygen. On a second trip the oxygen gave no relief, but phenacetine did. The fourth ascent was free from the sickness, the author being in "prime condition ".on the summit.

div.head: WOMEN'S CHAT.
div.p: WOMEN'S CHAT.

The King as Agriculturist.—The King was, as nsnal,a successful exhibitor at the Royal Agricultural Show which was visited by His Majesty, the Queen, and the Prince of \Vales. The King is not only a good judge of high-bred stock, but is a practical agriculturist, much more so than many of the great landowners, who figure as farmers, but only in the sense that they have estates upon which there are farms. Over the door of the King's Sandringham residence, is the inscription " this house was built by Albert Edward and Alexandra his wife, and the same might be said with regard to the creation of the horaefarm there, which extends to over 2,000 acres, and probably rears more high-bred stock than any other farm in the country. Originally, the farming prospects on the Sandringham estate were con- sidered extremely poor, but the home farm has been brought to such perfection that it is considered to be without equal. The interest of the Royal Family in agriculture is not, however, shared by the London public, which would scarcely know anything about the Show at Park Royal, except for the numbers of country people it brines to the metropolis for their summer visit. About Maids of Honour.—Society has frequently had a difficulty in distinguishing between the Vivian twins, and their twin cousins—the twin sisters—the Hon. Dorothy, and the Hon. Violet Vivian, are the daughters of Louisa Lady Vivian, and are both Maids of Honour to the Queen. Their twin cousins Miss Alberta, and Miss Alexandra Vivian, are the daughters of Lord Swan- sea, and are goddaughters, and namesakes of the King and Queen. The engagement recently announced, refers to that of the Hon. Dorothy Vivian, to Major-General Douglas Haig. There was a previous announcement, of; a similar kind about a year ago, but that engagement was afterwards broken off. A dowry of a thousand pounds was given on her marriage to each Maid of Honour by our late Queen, but that rule no longer obtains. A departing Maid also carried away her badge of office—a brooch consisting of a miniature of her Royal mistress, set in diamonds. In former times a Maid of Honour was regarded as a little more than a superior sort cf servant, but Court life is very different now, and, though the office may be something of a sinecure, the Maid of Honour must be exceedingly well read and accomplished, as she is brought into contact with till sorts of illustrious and distinguished people. Old Fashioned Names.—The Diike and Duchess of Norfolk have named their daughter Mary Rachel, a striking exception to the modern practice of avoiding the simple old-fashioned names for girls. Mary, it is true, is still a very common name in Roman Catholic families, but Rachel is not often met with, except among the Quaker community. But for many years past, the names of the Old Testament have been neglected, and if a girl is christened SUSW7, Jane, Anne, or Eliza, it is more than probable that she belongs to a high-born family. Other classes, less elevated in the social scale, have long discarded the old-fashioned names, and their places have been taken by Vera, Gladys, Gwendoline, Ivy, Viola, Irene, Rita, and others of a high-sounding, and more fashionable tone. Three Great Roman Catholic Houses.—The Duke and Duchess of Norfolk would have been better pleased with a son and heir, but any sentiment on that score has not affected the joyous welcome extended to their little daughter. Her arrival leaves questions of vast inheritance much as they were, the Duke of Norfolk's heir being his brother, Lord Edmund Talbot. His daughter, however, may eventually inherit the Herries title, and become a Baroness of Scotland in her own right. Lord Herries has no son, and therefore his elder daughter, the Ditchess of Norfolk, is heiress presump- tive to the ancient Scottish barony. Her, sister, the Hon. Mrs. Eric Drummond, who was one of last year's brides, and also has a little daughter, stood next in order of succession, but this place is now taken by the Duke of Norfolk's little girl. The Herries are not only closely related to the Howatds, but also to the wealthiest of the noble Roman Catholic families, the Crichton- Stttarts, Lady Herries, and the Marchioness of Bute the mother of the present Marquis—being sisters. One of Tortune's Favourites.—The Marquis of Bute is one of fortune's favourite% as is also his bride, the daughter of Sir Henry and Lady Bellingham, and the great social world has been much interested in the wedding, and accompanying festivities, at Castle Bell- ingham, in Ireland. The Marquis not only possesses a dozen titles, but owns nearly 120,000 acres of land, and the tenantry on the various estates have presented the happy pair with some valuable wedding gifts. It is close npoa five years since he succeeded to the title and estates of his father, which were valued at over five millions, and make the Marquis not only the highest peer in Scotland, but also one of the wealthiest men in the kingdom. His place Mochrum Castle in Wigtown- shire, where part of the honeymoon is to be spent, is not one of Lord Bate's ancestral seats, as it was pur- chased by the late Marquis from the Dunbars. His principal seat in Scotland is Mount Stuart about five miles from Rothesay, and is said to have cost not less than a million of more;. Women as Income Tax Payers.—The report of the Committee on Income Tax does not suggest any of the reforms for which many people were looking, but on the other hand points to harsher and more inquisitorial methods on the part of collectors. When the system of collecting the income tax was devised, any income or property that came to the wife really belonged to the husband, and as income tax payers, they were made one And indivisible. But all this has been altered by the Married Women's Property Acts,and the entry of women generally into the professions and occupations of life. If a man and a woman have each £3OO or £4OO a year, they are entitled to substantial drawbacks, as separate tax payers, but if they marry,these allowances are with- drawn. This is not as it should be, especially seeing that the tendency in these days among both men and women, is to avoid entering upon the cares and respon- sibilities of setting up housekeeping. The Fashionable Handkerchief.—With the departuie of the pouched blouse, and the sleeve ending in a baggy arrangement at the wrist. the stowing away of the handkerchief is a difficult task. Many women tuck the little square of cambric into the waist belt, but it must he remembered that unless of very small dimensions this would cause an unsightly bulge. The newest hand- kerchiefs however, which are edged with lace, and shew medallions in the corners, are only about six inches square, and these can be quite easily stowed away in the belt, in the folds of the blouse,in the top of the long glove, or the opening of the short varieties. Many women are having tiny handkerchief,and "puff" pockets arranged in the frills, or the more modish ruche, that finishes off the elbow sleeve, but it must be admitted that they are not altogether a success. Children's Bathing Dress.—No child should pay its annual visit to the seaside without its own bathing dress which by the way, should always be well rinsed in fresh water after use. For little folks, the stockinette bath- ing dress is unquestionable the best, in a medium or dark shade of blue, and where the tunic is deemed a desirable addition, it should be well stitched on, to save the uncomfortable dragging of sperate garments. Many of the new bathing dresses show short puffed sleeves, gathered into tight bands, the knickers being finished off in the same way. For bobbing up and down a couple of feet of water, the idea is all very well, and decidedly pretty, hut for swimming such a fashiou should be left severely alone. There should be nothing tight about the dress, and nothing to impede the free action of the limbs. After stockinette, a thin light weight, serge is the best choice for bathing dresses for the little folks ; linen an cotton " strike cold," and therefore should never be selected for such a purpose. Millinery Fruit.—At a fashionable and crowded fun - lion, held the other day,a man was heard to remark that "dessert is much worn on the head," and undoubtedly the milliners are favouring fruit just now to a consider- able degree. Cherries are perhaps the leading choice, but currants, plums, peaches and apples, are all having 11 great vogue,

div.head: SIMPLE FROCK.
div.p: A SIMPLE FROCK.

A pale pink-and-white checked zephyr is dui primary suggestion for the simple frock shown in the sketch. The chief feature is the large pointed collar of embroidered linen. These collars can now be bought complete with a collar band, and can be obtained in a variety of shapes. They look very pretty when used as yokes for dresses or blouses. The blouse bodice is made unlined, and is fastened behind. We would suggest that the collar be placed over the blouse before the sleeves are set in, and it

should be well stitched down, great care being taken to arrange the fulness nicely, and then, if liked, the material can be cut away from behind and the edges made neat. The sleevcs are arranged in two puffs to the elbow, each puff divided by a band of the material. The two full frills are simply hemmed at the edges. The skirt is slightly gathered at the waist, and is trimmed with tiny frills, headed with narrow bands; these would he better made complete first and then stitched to the skirt.
"STITCH, STITCH, SITICH !"

A correspondent writes to the Lady's fictorial : Ladies are not often able to estimate the number A stitches they work into the various household trticles they make from time to time. A Cambridge tady has, however, succeeded in reckoning the :otal of stitches she has worked into two quilts, Ind the figures are extremely interesting. In one trticle there are 1,060 pieces, each of which has 1,332 stitches, and with the number in the border work the total reaches 1,618,023. The 320 pieces In the second quilt each contain 3,172 stitches, Ind in the entire covering there are altogether 1,216,176. Therefore the total number of stitches al the two quilts reaches the extraordinary figure )f 2,834,199, or nearly 3,000,000.

LADY LOAFERS. " There may be male loafers, superabundant male Loafers, but it seems to me, writes Mrs. John Lane in the Fortnight/y, as if their united numbers are as aothing compared to those worthy lady loafers who ire perfectly respectable and perfectly idle. Why ihould a woman be permitted to loaf unreproved? Is idleness a feminine privilege?

div.head: WHITE SERGE COSTUME.
div.p: WHITE SERGE COSTUME.

The world is thinking of, and preparing for. its annual holiday, and the feminine part is thinking of holiday clothes. For the majority this summer outing means a trip to the seaside, and for seaside wear nothing is so suitable as serge. Blue serge for the morning and white for the afternoon is tho maxim of many sea- side girls, and, having this in mind, 'our sketch shows a smart but inexpensive little costume .in white serge. The Eton coat is finished with double collars and revers of embroidered silk outlined with straps of stitched glace, the short sleeves being finished with a cuff to match.

and a frill of accordion-pleated silk. The skill is a seven-gored one, having a seam down the centre of the front and a box-pleat at the back. Each seam is machine-stitched, and opens to- wards the bottom to shew a pleating of the white glace silk. If this gown is beyond the purse of the would-be possessor. the inlets of pleated silk might be easily omitted, and this would considerably reduce the cost. In this case the seams would be stitched all the way down in the usual way. HUSIIkNI/5 AND WIVES.

div.head: CHAPTER NORMWARDS.
div.p: CHAPTER NORMWARDS.

LADY AGNES CU= had disoppeared as completely as though the ground had swal- lowed her up. She had left thrt house about Six o'clock without the knowledge of her parents. One of the gardeneis had seen her cross the lawn, and go down through the gate into the park. The evening was a fine one, but there appeared to be no reason why she should have chosen to take a walk so late in the afternoon, _

It was probable thei efore that she, had gone out on some special errand. One of the foot- men, on being questioned by Lord Heather- stone, reported that he had handed her a letter about 3.30. It had e.ome in by the afternoon post. No trace of the letter could be found in her bedroom, anel she had evi- dently destroyed it or taken it with her. No special notice wa's. taken of her absence till dinner time, when she failed to put in an appearance. The search commenced at once and continued all night, and the whole ot the next day. Messengers were despatched in every direction in the hope of fin:ling someone who had seen her. But they brought back no information, and the searchers in. the park found no traces of a struggle, Or anything that would point to an act of violence. But late that afternoon a sailor, rather the worse for liquor, came up to the Hall and re- ported that about six o'clock the . previous evening he had seen a large motor ear running along the road at the foot of the park. It was too dark for him to distinguish the number of the occupants, or even the colour of the car. He further explained, with a tinge of pride, that he was in no fit state to see anything clearly, having just returned from a . long voyage, and having spent most of the previous day in the "Plough and Sail" at Gorehaven.

This news, told somewhat incoherently. sent a thrill of horror through those who listened to the speaker. There was no doubt in anyone's mind that Lady Agnes had fallen into the hands of the arc:ll-ruffian William Jordison. There appeared, however, to be no reason for her abduction, unless it had been carried out in the hope of obtaining a ransom. This method of obtaining money did not seem practicable in a civilised and open country. It w=',l possible in the mountains of Spain or Greece, but hardly to be imagined in the lanes and marshes of Essex. The next morning, however, two people knew why Lady Agnes had disappeared. Both Lady Heather-stone and Arthur Holme received letters from JOrdison himself. They had been posted from C7p Withing, a small village in Yorkshire, and were somewhat similar in their contents. . - •

_ ...... -.......__ _ One, which would have certainly surprised Lord Heatherstone, ran as follows : " Dear Marie,— "It may be possible to strike you through the death of one you love. One day 1 hope to strike a harder and more final blow.— Lady Heatherstone burnt the letter and was silent as to its contents. The other ran taus:—

"Dear Mr. Holme,— " The life of the woman you love is in my hands. You know the price of her release. —W. J ." This letter was brought out to Arthur Holme as he was spending a few days on the " Rover" preparatory to the start of his cani paign in Gloucestershire. From the bearer of it he heard the first news of the disappearance' of Lady Agnes Cliffe., He hurriedly thrust some things in a bag, returned in the man's boat, and drove thirty miles to Heatherstone Hall.

- Lord Hcatherstone received him in the library, and told him the little that was known about the affair. In return Artkur Holme handed him the letter. The Earl read it through twice, and then glanced keenly at the young man. So Jordison is alive," he said," and it was one of his seavrnts who perished in the fire." "It seems so," Holine replied. "Do you know Jordison's writing ? Lord Heatherstone asked.

answered Holine frankly, " I do not. This may be the workof some practical joker." "it can be easily verified" said Lord Heatherstone. " What price ooes this nran expect you to pay? Did you ever meet him before you came across him at the Red House ?." And Lord Koatherstone watched Holme's face carefully as he asked the ques- tion.

"Never," Holme replied, emphatically. He's a madman, and wishes .to know, some- thing which lam unable to tell him." . "Then he. has no real cause for disliking you " " None whatever," Holme replied, but he turned his eyes away from Lord Heather- stone's keen gaze a's he answered the question. He knew very well why Jordison disliked him. The shifting of the eyes did not escape Lord Heatherstone's notice, and he made a mental note that Holme had told hint a he. !' div.head: ELECTRIC VACUUM VALVES.
div.p: ELECTRIC VACUUM VALVES.

"Electric vacuum valves," originally suggested by the late Sir George Gabriel Stokes a long time ago, have the property of acting as accumulators for high tension intermittent currents, and a steady current of high tension can, it seems, be obtained from them. These currents can be utilised for pro- ducing X-rays, serve instead of comparatively small coils for storing electric impulses, and other uses of high tension continuous currents. Sir Oliver Lodge contemplates their application to the dissipation of metallic fumes and fogs.

div.head: GLASS THAT NO HEAT CAN BREAK.
div.p: GLASS THAT NO HEAT CAN BREAK.

Glass that can be heated white hot and then plunged.into cold water without breaking would seem an impossibility, but it has been made an accomplished fact. It is made from Brazilian quartz pebbles, heated red hot and then thrown into dis- tilled water. Then the purest pieces are selected and welded with the oxyhydrogen blowpipe intc long stems like straws, from which glass vessels of any shape can be made. Thus far this quartz glass has been employed chiefly for making laboratory apparatus. A test tube, however thin, made in this way will not break when a white-hot coal is dropped into it.

div.head: CANNON TO PREVENT HAILSTORMS.
div.p: CANNON TO PREVENT HAILSTORMS.

The idea that heavy artillery tiring is productive of rain is an old one, and cases are recorded where great battles have been followed by heavy showers. This has been one of the methods practised by the modern rain-maker. But the firing of cannon has been more usefully employed for the keeping off of hailstorms. It is found that the storm cloud may be broken up and dispersed in this way. In the wine-growing district of Beaujolais, in Central France, cannon firing for the prevention of hail- storms has been systematically carried out for a number of years. And evidence is now brought forward to show that the five years, 1900 to 1904, during which it has been practised compare favour- ably with the previous years, 1891 to 1900. It is also said that thunder and lightning are frequently suppressed within the region while raging outside it. As a practical proof of belief in is efficiency it may be mentioned that there are no fewer than twent% -eight societies for dispersing hailstorms by cannon firing within the district.

div.head: STRANGE CABLE BREAKDOWNS.
div.p: STRANGE CABLE BREAKDOWNS.

On November 6th, 1901, the cable which connects Valdez and Sitka, Alaska, broke down. On testing it, the break was located about ten miles from Sitka. When the cable was handed up, it was found to have captured a whale 50ft. long. A loop of the cable passed round the lower jaw, and held it fast. The strands of the cable were much torn and twisted, and there were several breaks in the conductors. Probably the whale, swimming with open mouth, had unintentionally taken the cable, which lay suspended on the irregularities of the bottom, in its Jaws. Only one other case of a whale interrupting a cable service is recorded, and that was •in the Red Sea many years ago. In this case, the tail of the cetacean was caught in a loop of the cable. A case is recorded, however, of a pair of eagles which stopped the electric supply service of Fresno, in California. The machinery at the station was quietly sending on electricity at 10,000 volts, when the service was suddenly interrupted. After going over a considerable length of wire, the surveying party reached the top of a mountain, five miles from the power-house. There they found the cause of the disaster in the shape of the charred remains of two eagles. Ihese birds, alighting on two adjacent parts of the three-phase current, must have touched each other, and formed a short circuit. The electric current rushed through them, and they were thus cremated. 1!

div.p: PENKETH PARISH AFFAIRS.
A Mortuary Wanted.

A special meeting of the Penketh Parish Council wee held in the Wesleyan schools on Monday evening, Dr. Murray, presiding. There were also present :—Messrs. W. Hodgkinson, D. Houghton, R. Routledge, J. Ditch- field, and E. Forster (clerk.)

div.head: RECREATION GROUND.
div.p: THE RECREATION GROUND.
It was stated that at a meeting of the Council in committee tender of Mr. J. Edgerley for the supply of gymnastic apparatus for the recreation ground was accepted. THE DANGERS OF SANKEY STATION.

--- • The Chairman said the Sankey Parish Council had recently been making efforts to obtain new booking arrangements at Sankey Station to obviate the necessity of crossing the line. Considerable correspondence had taken place and the manager for the Cheshire Lines Committee had visited the station. Dr. Murray sugge:ted that it would strengthen the movement if the Council passed a resolution urging the need for an alteration. _ . . .

Hodgkinson: It concerns penketh quite as much as Sankey. The Chairman: I should say more so. There are more travellers from Penketh than from Sankey. The Chairman said, the Sankey Council got "no forrader" in the matter until recently when Mr. Pinion, the manager, came down, and seemed to take a more favourable view.

The Clerk said the Penketh Council had hitherto been successful in approaching public bodies, and they might be equally so in the present instance. Mr. Hodgkinson said there was a strong feeling in Penketh that the improvement should be carried out. On the motion of Mr. Routledge, seconded by Mr. Hodgkinson, the Clerk was instrnoted to write the Cheshire Lines Committee emphasising the need for an •dteration.

WARRINGTON ROAD. A letter was read from Mr. J. C. Sutton, clerk to the Rural District Council, stating that at a meeting of that authority the surveyor was instructed to see the Surveyor with a view to the possible carrying out of the request of the Parish Council for the paving and flagging of Warrington-road. ' APPLICATION FOR INCREASED REMUNERATIO'N. Mr. Thos. Whitfield, dust contractor, having applied to the Rural District Council for increased remunera- tion, the matter was referred to the Parish Council for discussion. The Chairman said Mr. Whitfield applied for an increase of £l5 twelve months ago, but the Parish Council considered such an advance would be premature, and the salary was raised by £7 10s. At present it stood at £92 10s. After discussion it was decided that the District Council be requested to postpone consideration of the application for twelve months. At the same time the Council desired to express its commendation of the very satisfactory manner in which the work had been done. MR. 1). HOUGHTON'S THANKS.

Walking Day in the past has been singularly free from accidents but this year, unfortunately, the same cannot be written as an accident of a serious nature happened to a child attending the Work- ingmen's Mission. Early in the day the scholars proceeded to a field at Burtonwood in lorries. When one of the lorries was entering the farm a little girl named;Aruy Rickers,daughter of,Mr. Enoch ftickers,Well- field-street, in her excitement fe,l to the ground, the wheel of the lorry passing over chest. She WAS at once conveyed to the Infirmar_ where it was found that she was suffering from severe internal injuries. For some time she lay in an extremely critical condition but later reports are to the effect that she is now progressing favourably.

their conduct of the business with which for so many years he had been so happily connected. The firm had always inspired one with the belief that mere money- making was not their sole aim. The instances were I many in which if this trait alone had controlled their actions many good deeds that stood to -their credit world never have been done. Reverting to the business of the moment he thanked them for the kind things Mr. Groves had been pleased to say. They valued his good opinion for therein lay the success of their business. They trusted to merit that good opinion and to recipro- , cite it by devoting attention to customers' interests. ' Most of them would .remember the small beginnings of I years ago. He was glad to say that the business con- tinued to prosper, and while it was agreeable to be ! identified with success, it was a pleasant reflection to all to feel that in their several capacities they had in some degree contributed to that success. Possibly many of them had heard of contemplated changes, ana wondered to what they were leading. Though matters were not ripe for a full disclosure, this much he might venture to say, that the changes would add materially to their resources for extending their manufactures, and as i these changes would involve an increased demand for labour there would be a benefit to the town they were 1 all so proud to belong to. Continuing. Mr. Henshall said he felt they should not let that occasioa pass with- I out offering to Mr. R. A. Naylor their best wishes tor - his success in the political venture he has so courage- ously embarked upon in the district in which they stood. He was sure that if Mr. Naylor brought to bear upon the contest those qualities of head and heart, that they knew so well he possessed, then there could be only one result —success would attend his efforts. From time to time he had occasion to visit the six Carnarvon Boroughs of which that ancient town of Criccieth is not the least important. and wherever he had gone he had heard of • the enthusiasm Mr. .Naylor inspired in his journeys I througn the constituency; and from friend and opponent alike he had heard golden opinions of Mr. Naylor's character and amiability in conducting his candidature , to what they hoped would be a successful issue. If these 1 opinions were any criterion of the progress Mr. Naylor, was making, then he felt justitied in taking a hopeful , view of his chances, and outsiders who are inclined to , look upon Mr. Naylor's candidature as a forlorn hope, might meet with a surprise. If he might presume to advise their friends in Criccieth and the other royal and ancient boroughs, he would say that they would honour themselves if they secured as their future member, Mr. Naylor, whom they know as one of nature's gentlemen, a God-fearing man, possessing those estimable qualities ' and abilities, which when conjoined, made him an ideal member for any, constituency. He was sure all present , heartily wished Mr. Naylor the best of luck, and another I year it might be their pleasure to tender him their hearty congratulations as member for the constituency. Mr. Edwards (cashier) also spoke, and expressed the I hope that all the excursionists had thoroughly enjoyed their visit to a district which he hoped before long would be represented by Mr. R. A. Naylor ; he WAS quite qualified to represent it. He had heard words spoken that day which led him to believe that his chances were not as hopeless as some would lead them to believe. (Hear, hear.) Mr. Shakeshaft said he did not know that he could add anything to what had been already said. Had Mr. Naylor been present he would have joined heartily in all the proceedings of the day as all of them had done. lie had shown his interest in them by the telegram which had been read, lie was ; sure he would be pleased to know that they had had such an enjoyable day. It would be better not to say too much about politics in that particular district, but at the same time, they all wished him 8113CPSS. (p- -please.) Judging from the feeling of the town Mr. I Naylor stood a good chance. He hoped that whatever could be done in his favour would be done. (Hear, hear.)

Councillor Forshaw said it was his unexpected as well as his pleasing duty to say a few words on that interesting occasion. That was the first time he had had the pleasure of accompanying the employes on that annual trip, but he hoped It would not be the last time. (Hear, hear.) It was true the journey to Criccieth had been a long one, but the beautiful surroundings of the district had amply recompensed them for it. In company with the other , visitors, he very sincerely and heartily thanked Mr. Naylor for his hospitality. They knew that the firm of K. A. Naylor had the highest reputation. It had a world-side renown. They also know that Mr. Naylor was a splendid business man, and that the name of Robert Anderton Naylor was becoming a household word in the Carnarvon boroughs. He was sure he would make a splendid representative. He would not only represent the people by his tongue, but he would bring to bear his business capabilities in its interests. (Hear, hear.) He admired Mr. Lloyd-George for his ability, and also because he was a brother solicitor, but of the two men the better Parliamentary repre- sentative for the district would be Mr. Naylor. (Applause.) He hoped that when they came to Car- narvon again he would have the pleasnre of addressing Mr. Naylor as the member for the district. A Voice: "We will have von as a canvasser.") English people admired the Wel.sh people for their loyalty to the King. They had a beautiful country. England was their (the Welshmen's) country, as well as the Englishmen's. They were a united people, and he was convinced that if they

()owing to the holidays there was only a moderate • attendance at this meeting on Sunday last. Mr. A. Healey presided, and spoke upon "Thankfulness to God for our spared lives." Mr. C. Rose from Manchester based his address on incidents in Naaman's cure of his leprosy, showing how in doing what the Prophet told him he put his own ideas o one side. The lesson to be d n derived was that they must come to God not ire their own way but in God's appointed way; then all were accepted and none rejected. The Rev. John Yonge (the President) after giving a hearty welcome to a new member, made reference to the death of Mr. Dirchall, J.P., who had passed away in his 75th year. Mr. Birchall was willing to help in every good work that suggested itself to his mind. He was not one to push himself to the front, but was always ready to give all the help he could. During their 12 years of P.S.A. work, Mr. Birchall was always a great friend of the movement, and often presided at its meetings. Mr. Farrar seconded the vote of condolence.. He said he had known and worked with Mr. Birchall for many years in many ways, and had always found him ready to give a helping band to everything for the benefit of xvorkicgmen. He bad risen from the ranks by his attention to duty, and ability in business' and by the blessing of God and his fidelity to Him, had gained a position of honour and respect in the town of his birth. —The vote was passed by the brethren standing up in their places.

It was very curious, says " Belle " in the " to watch, at Grosvenor House, the Japanese suite of Prince and Princess Arisugawa, some of whom were very little men, and had, in consequenca of their position,to go into supper with some of our very stately, well-grown ladies of high rank. The Duchess of Port- land and the Duchess of Marlborough, in particular, were sent in with very small cavaliers. A lady who was cycling near Bexhill felt something strike her head, and found that a sparrow in its fight across the road had impaled itself on her hatpin, which. was protruding about two inches. This bird died from its injury. On Saturday Sarah Ann Thorne, wife of an Alderholt, Dorset, fanner, threw herself into the river, but was rescued by a young man named Albert Hood. Charged with attempted suicide at Wimborne on Monday, prisoner Said," It's all brought on by worrying over tl;es children." She was bound over.

div.head: EXAMINEE JULY Ilth 1905.
div.p: THE EXAMINEE JULY Ilth 1905.

EVEN the Goverc- THE PREMIER AND meat cannot lose THE COUNTRY. every seat, so Mr BALFOUR may .draw ' a little chastened comfort from Kingswinford although the Unionist majority has dropped a thousand. But to do. him justice, Mr. BALFOUR is not greatly moved either by good fortune or the reverse in the bye-elections. All he cares about is
his majority from dty to day in the House of
'Commons. At prebent Mr. BALFJUR'S mind is engaged with other matter. There is the closure of the Aliens Bill. That singularly ill-drama measure

is to be reed a third time within a fortnight. It is not designed to cope with an evil of any magnitude . for in spite of:Mr. BOAR LAW'S figures the num- ber of immigrant aliens is small. What the 'Government hope is that the Bill will do them ',some good in the constituencies. Their calcula- tion is altogether misplaced. Most people regard . the Bill as a patrol for Mr. Cutterieritexer's policy 't --a construction wok!) he has not hesitated to put ',• Upon it. Any Liberal G wernment would be .o.enite prepared to exclude the really undesiie • able alien—the criminal alien, the deceased alien—and that is why the Bill was not op- posed on the second reading. But if it should pass without special amendment it will, keep out any decent and competent foreigner who cannot Produce a definite contract of employment which Will ensure his subsistence from the moment of , landing. This is an extreme course. for which no 7.7.mecessity has been proved. Mr. Bs:Leona admits ~•-,, that this will happen under the Bill, but he dis- k Missed such a case as an exception which need not tr. 'be considered in any broad scheme of policy, and f-I 'rather than remedy the drawing of the Bill he ' will carry the whole of it by closure. This is characteristic, but what good it will do 'him in the country even his electioneering agents would be puzzled to say. His journals affect to believe that the closure is welcomed by public 'Opinion as a proof of his determination and capa- city to transact the business of the country. This is as if a man were to plead that he is doing what be assumes to be your business, when your sole desire is to get rid of him altogether. That is how we read public opinion, as expressed ‘ 'by the only part of the constitutional machinery . Which is beyond Hr. BALFOUR'S control. It would be sinaply frankness in his supporters to admit , that he continues to rule by his arbitrary construe : tion of the-Septennial Act. But some of them are aasuring us now that he is going to endear himself -still more to public opinion by the moderation of ;,. his views about redistribution. It may turn out, :" they say, tfiat tot thirty Irish seats are to be ~. , 'extinguished but only eighteen. This marvellous forethought will not affect the situation in the :c‘ least. The Opposition simply affirm that if any- body is to handle redistrilsution Mr. BALFOUR is 7t tot the man. , . The politicians who should be extinguished are not the Irish thirty, or eighties,or any other num" bar, hut the men who keep Mr. 13.1Lroun in office in defiance of the country. This is the conclusive argument against everything Mr. BaLroult. does. It invalidates his authority at every point, and is a sufficient reason why the Opposition need not -trouble themselves about the daily fulminations Realest what are called their obstructive tactics. The use which the Prime Minister has made of the ''•ePtennial Act relieves them from any obligation to smooth the way for any Government business for the rest of the session, or for next year, sup. PoSing that Mr.l3eLeoun has the assurance to meet 'Parliament next year as head of a Ministry with bo Moral authority whatever. • ,We feel that an appreciation of the late Mt ehomas Birched is due from us for several special reasons. In the first place Mr. Birchen was a man Whom the town, and the "Examiner," delighted 'to honour. He was one of Warringtou's most Worthy sons and leaves behind him a record of 'Public and private service which it is given to few ;Ilea to equal. Mr. Birchen had too, an indirect out close connection with the "Examiner.' As a -atree , g politician he always supported the paper of party, and was never better pleased than when, , ,111.LIny years ago, his only son joined the „.„-0.. 3 ttaminer "staff as a reporter. The subsequent ..-e- u°, a ess of Mr. Fred Birchall—now holding an ... %Portant position in American journalism— ,l forded a satisfaction to his father in which we ',llvo always been pleased to share. Mr. Birchen waes one of natiirt,'s gentlemen and largely blessed with those attributes of character which earn for a loan the enduring esteem of his fellows. , Tnesday's comparatively light agenda nroved no Pbarbmger of a brief meeting of the Warrington 2%1.1 Council. Tne three-hour limit, which we ,I'leggested a month ego, was again exceeded, arid ..iroe of the discussions were decidedly scrappy. .tea,arle an hour was expended in arguing over a t"'irta-five-year-old beam engine at Winwick which 4 .118 Water Committee proposes to spend £1,600 0". Very few members displayed much know- °, p of engines, beam or otherwise, though one ,Ae‘vvo spoke familiarly and even tenderly of the ,u 4. tiervant at Winw.ek as " she." Tne genera 1,1211,1i0n seemed in favour of sending the minutes .atZkt, for the expenditure of so large a sirn on a ec °Biled-by engine was not welcome. ilewever te e " carried her pout when a show of hands 8-0490 taken, the Mayors vote just turning the '9. Seeing that opinion in the Council was so bl:_ally divided, His Worship might very properly .e_nve. used his deciding vote in favour of a re- Is. .ei;. sid.eration of the matter. Expenditure at 4, a,l_nwick and Delph-lane somehow seems fated to ".. .. PPear excessive, whether the facts warrant such . tui assumption or not. ~. , ' cull',l3o%Enc.)st important debate of the evening, that ncillor Pemberton's motion, was also centred : -.cowl_aterworks expenditure. For somethine like - et years now, Councillor Pemberton has • '"Reled with indomitable persistence to obtain Particulars f tract a 0 the work done under Lawson'a con- the amount of extras involved. One iii.:!vhaeratve naturally thought that, as a member of Committee, Councillor Pemberton's (see to check the work done would have been We can see no reason why he, or any
I

' other meinnce. of the Committee, should not have I been given every opportauity of examining the work and revising the charges if he so desired. There need he no sug,gestioa of everything not k, being straightforward in the just demand of a Councillor to personally supervise important public works, and it was clearly in the interest of the Water Committee and the contractor they employed to allow Councillor Pemberton the most ample facilities for investigation. So far as we are aware he has not made any request for particalars, specifi cations, bills of quantities aud the like, which could for any sound reason be refused. To-day, the ,works stand practically completed and much of the investigation which Couucillor Pemberton desired to make is quite impossible. Whether this is to the advantage of the Water Committee is open to doubt. As a Cminittee they do net stand well with the public. A huge amount of money hes been expended at Win wick and Dalph- lane upon which there has been absolutely no check and shoot which the pnblic knows very little Economies to the extent of hundreds of pounds ! might hey.) been possible, and how many members of the Water Committee can honestly assert that they were not? Alderman Francomb stated that no member of the Council has seen the conditions of Lawson's contract. This is a serious admission, and reflects unfavourably on the thoroughness of the members of his committee. They ought to have known a good deal about a contract of £24,000 before letting it to anyone, and they ought also to have taken a more direct and personal interest in the carrying out of that contract. Apparently Councillor Pemberton is the only member wile has evinced any desire to sliver- visa the work in the way that every man would do were the expenditure of his own money involved. We hope he will persevere in his endeavour to dispel the:dense fog which obscures the carrying out of the racent important and expensive exten• sinus of the waterworks undertaking.

Now that Mr. Howarth, the sub:librarian,has received an appointment at Chelensfbed, the War- rington Council is beginning to value \his services. The discussion on the Library Cammittee's minutes revealed, the fact that many members are in favour of some effort being made to retain Mr. Howarth's services. No resolution on the matter was proposed, however, and in all probability Mr. Howarth ivill take up the very ranch hotter apnointment he has received in the oretty town of Chelmsford. Rather curiously the Library here is one of those provided fly Mr. Carnegie and is not yet flushed. Mr. Howarth will thus have a brand-new building in his charge and be able to organise the Chelmsford Library cm the most modern lines. We beieve Chelmsford will find him an excellent public servant. In Warring- ton, while his services were fully appreciated, his labours were very poorly recompensed. Ericy a sub-librarian of 13 vesrs standing in the Dapart- ment, w;th only £l2O a year We have not for , gotten Mr. Howerth's application for an increased salary a f. 14, years ago and the Committee's response. If we are not mistaken he was granted the munificent sum of 2s. per week ex;ra. No wonder he has been anxious f.)r a change! The committee, notwithstanding its limited ineofne, is apparently capsble of dealing more generously with its servants foe we note that Mr. Howarth's successor will automatically reach tne salary he relik,qaishes in four years from his appointment. Even then he will not be over-peid, hut he will be doing much better than was Mr. Howarth. We wish the latter every success in the E3SOX county town.

Many psonle are asking when the Warrington and South Lancashire Memorial to Fa,len Soldiers, of which a great deal was heard a few months ago, is going to take stthstantial shone. We are informed that Mc. Alfred Drury, A.R A, has the sketches in hand, and that the designs w,ll he sulomitted to the committee in due course. We hope that wh n the time is ripe the request of the Workingmen's Committee that Sir Radvers Biller should tie invited to unveil the memorial, will receive favourable consideration. Amongst popular heroes, Sir R Avers holds a foremost place in the estimation of his fellow-countrymen, and a genuine Lancashire welcome would await him if he honoured the "good old town" with a visit.

The visions of self-4overnment which have hen tempting the croo.i people of Stockton Heath will probably be rudely dispelled by the report on the subject which has been presented to the Parish Council. The committee have discovered that th 3 funds at the disposal of an urban authority would, unless the rates were increased, amount to only £1,400 per annum, and if the " Heathens" cat. run the authority on that sum they will indeed be the envy of less brilliant administrators. The Parish Council, however, admlt that such a task is beyond them, and have regretfully come to the conclusion that urban powers will not pay. 'De ratepayers have the final voice in the matter, but we imagine that little will he heard of the desire for urban powers when the pros and cons have been fully discussed in the village.

Mr. Balfour has seen lit to convey his congratu- lations to the promoters of the recent Chamber- lain meeting at St. Helens, at which a resolution in favour of Colonial precenence w naised. £l4 tells Sir Henry Sltou Karr : " That meeting appears to have been a mist brilliant success, aid I hope you will convey to those who organised it my warmest congratulations." This being so, Mr. Arthur Illiott pertinently asks in the "Times " : "Is it possible to affirm any longer that Mr. Balfour, the leader of the Conservative party, is opposed to the policy of Mr. Chamberlain and of the Tariff Reform L8.1g114. You do not congratu- late the organiser of a demonstration in favour of policy- unless you agree with the policy." The electors have long since been convinced that Mr. Balfour and Mr. Chamberlain stand for one and the same thing—Protection—and it is that palicy which they are so actively resisting at the polls.
