div.head: DEATH OF MR. CHARLES BIRCHALL.
div.p: DEATH OF MR. CHARLES BIRCHALL.

One of Liverpool's best-known public men passed away on Tuesday in the person of Mr. Charles Birchall, proprietor of the" Liverpool Journal of Commerce," who died at his residegce. The Laurels, Egremont, at the age of sixty-two. Mr. Birchall was one of the most popular men in the city and in the Wallasey district. His increasing activity in connection with his business responsibilities compelled him to refuse offers for civic positions in Liverpool. as well as candidature for Par- liamentary honours; but he identified himself promin- ently with religious and philanthropic agencies. He was a Conservative in politics. Always genial, of buoyant spirits, and so large-hearted and generous to the poor and needy, his departure will be mourned throughout the district of Wallasey and in the city of his adoption. Mr. Birchall was twice married, and leaves a widow, son, and daughter. His son. Mr. C. Herbert Birchall, was managing director of the "Journal of Commerce" wben it was formed into a limited liability company a few years with the shares held between father and son, and theblatter now succeeds to to the business.

Warrington Coal Company Summoned. At the Warrington County Petty Sessions on Wednesday the Wigan Coal and Iron Co., Warrington branch, were summoned for having in their possession a pair of unjust scales.—lnspector McDonald said that on the 3rd June he saw one of the defendants' lurries at Sankey. Ile examined the scales and found that they varied from 8 to 14 ounces against the purchaser. —The scales were produced by the Inspector who showed that the scales varied according to the placing of the weights. At the request of Mr. Allen (lifessrs. Peace and Ellis) who defended, the weights were placed in different positions and it was shown that the scales could be u,ade to vary against the company. Mr. Allen submitted that the scales were correct and after a lengthy argument the case was dis- missed.—A second summons for a similar offence was also dismissed.—The company were then summoned in two instances with having in their possession weights which were light to the extent of 6.5 and 3 ounces, and also with having sacks containing coal to , which the necessary metal label was not attached Mr. Allen admitted technical offences and fines of 2s. 6d. and costs were inflicted in each case. An application by the police to have the weights con- fiscated was not granted it being- pointed out that the weights could be made correct.
The Examinet, Saturday, July 8, 1905.

div.head: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
div.p: NOTES AND NOTIONS.
"The birds have flown " from the Park Aviary and, of course, the worn-out top is now being quickly replaced.
Justice was dispensed with surprising rapidity at the Borough Police Court on Monday, forty cases being dealt with in the short space of an hour. Perhaps this constitutes a record ? * * *
While a brass band disC'oursed lively nmsic in an adjacent building, the Penketh Parish Council on Monday gravely discussed the advisability of provid- ing a mortuary for the parish, * * *

The liveliest and most protracted . discussion at the Council meeting on Tuesday was on Councillor Pemberton's motion respecting Lawson's contract at Dolph-lane, and the. man Num spoke oftenest and interrupted most waS the Mayor. This is not good chairmanship your Worship!

Mr. Carnegie has not yet been approached by War- rington for a Library grant. The nutter is "engaging the serious consideration of a sub-committee" which is to present a report in due course. IF the sub-com- mittee could contrive to forget the matter for a few )ears it would be doing the town a good service. * * * The result of the CorpratiOn Investigation Com- mittee's inquiries is being anxiiliasly awaited by the public. There should have been another meeting of the committee on Thursday, but we hear that as one ' of the chief parties concerned failed to put in an appearance, an adjournment had to be made. Can you draw a cow, a sheep, or a dog? If so impart the valuable knowledge you possess to your children if you have any. The committee of the Mid- Cheshire Show have decided to offer prizes for essays and freehand drawings on farm animals generally, to , be confined to children attending elementary schools within the area of the show. There ought to be some interesting contributions from the juveniles. * * There is a bye-law in Warrington which is framed for the punishment of the careless person who strikes matches on shop-fronts, but it has never been enforced. At Halifax.the police are evidently less fully occupied and can afford time to keep an eye on the promiscuous match-striker. On Tuesday it cost a Luddendenfoot young man 9s. Cal, for so thoughtlessly " lighting-up " in the hilly Yorkshire town. * * * The Library came ,in for more criticism at the Council meeting on Tuesday, but no one ventured to go quite so far as the worthy Bolton 'Councillor who ,on Wednesday described the libraries of that town as being "infested with ephemeral fiction and magazines, and contained thousands of books that should be chucked away or burned as waste." We tremble to think what Alderman Bennett would have said to such an indictment!

The plea which a Live-rpo:d corresp-mdant puts forth on behalf of the family cat is worthy of sympathetic attention. The writer points out how in many cases when paople depart for their: annual holiday they neglect to .make proper provision for the cat and 't turn it adrift to starve until it is reduced to eating what garbage it can find." It is suggested that the R.S.P.C.A. should prosecute some of those persona who systematically and thoughtlessly inflict thie common form of cruelty.

* ;* Distance seems to lend enchantment to the day trip —at least one would think so, judging from the long journeys which many of our local excursionists are pleased to undertake. They have not yet ventured so far afield as the cotton operatives of North-East Lancashire, who recently visited l3aulogne—but per- haps that will come in time. At present they. are content with outings to such places 'as Criccieth, Scarborough, and the Isle of Man—quite far enough, many will say, for one day. But then, the day trippers' energy, on this occasion at any rate, knows no bounds. * * *

Quite a remarkable instance of foresight has been disclosed in connectimi with the proposal to con- tinue the tram-tines for GO yards up Bridge-street. The street has to be repaved in the near future, and it is thought that there will be a saving if the train: lines are laid at the same time. Bravo somebody ! Perhaps the Gas and Water Committees can be per- suaded to do their little odd jobs at the same time. It will be quite refreshing to see the street repaved and not subsequently torn up piecenieal by two or three committees in turn.

In defending the Library on Tuesday Alderman Bennett had something to say of the =Clem novel. Most of the modern novels which everybody was clamouring for were " he said "forgotten in a year, so that if the Library Committee did not buy them at the commencement tlley generally found that. it was unnecessary to do so later." We have a good mind to tell Marie Corelli about our contemptuous alderman. She would probably give him a severer "wigging " than was bestowed upon the Lord Mayor of Leeds for venturing to disagree wi!,‘,ll A specially kind dispensation of Providence was requested for Walking Day—and denied. Warrington must have been in the black books, for the morning of the children's festival opened dull and showery, while there was only a slight improvement in the conditions as the day advanced. Never once did Old 5.11 show his kindly face. It was very unfortunate, and seemed particularly " hard lines " after such a spell of glori- ously sunny weather. No doubt mlst of the youngsters enjoyed themselves, but the depleted desks in the schools on Monday were eloquent testimony of the fact that coughs and colds had claimed many young victims. The percentage of absentees was quite abnormal,- and it is put down entirely to the effects of damp frocks and wet grass.

* * * ", Drunkenness," remarked the Pontefract Recorder on Monday, was greatly on the decrease. People could not walk about the world without noticing the fact, which was due to education and other humanising in- fluences." 71There are times, too,when one cannot help noticing that there is a good deal of drunkenness yet. On Thursday evening last week a visitor to Warring- ton would have thought the town a decidedly drunken place. especially if he were ignorant of the fact that it was the eve of Walking Day. In less than five minutes we encountered three drunken men staggering about Bridge street, and many other people seemed to have been preparing for Walking Day in similar fashion. The police were, of curse, in a state of benevolent oblivion.

_ * * * Despite all precautions taken for their safety, chil- dren somehow or other convive to get themselves into most dangerous situations, often with the saddest consequences. One would hardly have thought it possible for a child to fall into a reservoir enclosed by a wall nine feet high, but this was what actually happened at Bank Quay on Wednesday evening. Determined to be near the water, a number of children scaled the wall with the aid of a wire rope attiched to a telegraph post, and they were playing on a plank at the side of the reservoir when one of them slipped in and was drowned. It is, perhaps, almost useless to point the moral, though one would fain hope that such a painful affair might act as a warning to others not to rush so heedlessly into danger.

* Councillor John Roberts was quite eloquent at the Council meeting on the need for :a. new sand-blast machine for the Markets Committee. The old one, he said, had been in existence "ever since the birth of Adam:" It has always been understood that Adam was made and not born in the ordinary way, or per- haps like Topsy he " growed." Councillor Roberts was not in the least daunted by the laughter ho pro- voked and proceeded to further explain tlut the new machine " would be quite capable of doing away with one man." Again the Council laughed. The new machine is evidently going to be something out of the ordinary and cheap at SZO. Perhaps if it were pressed it might "do away with" several men who are not wanted. If necessary we will make out a short list for the Markets Committee !

* * • , There was a pretty passage at arms between Alder- men Bennett and Tinnien over the vexed question of physical drill instruction for the school children. Alderman Bennett informed the Chairman of the Gymnasium Committee that his attitude reminded him of the saying " Don't teach your grandmother to suck eggs." Alderman Tinnion retorted to the Chair- man of the Education Committee that he had thought for sometime that that Committee was grandmotherly but he did not like to put it so plainly. He added also that Alderman Bennett "knew as much about the subject as a sweep did about a clean shirt." The warfare between the two chairmen was getting some- what personal when the incident closed without either having yielded The Gymnasium Committee is not going ito give up its superintendence of physical drill among the school children without a struggle.

div.head: WATERWORKS CONTRACT.
div.p: THE WATERWORKS CONTRACT.
COUNCILLOR DEMANDS TO SEE ALL DOCUMENTS.
Alleged Excessive Extras.
HEATED DISCUSSION.

There was a heated discussion at Tnesday evening's meeting •of th) Warrington Town Council on tke following motions introduced by Councillor Pember- ton : —l, That Mr. Deas, the water engineer, shall show Councillor Pemberton all the papers, contracts, and letters in connecti na with Lawson's c intract at Delph-lane, any other member of the Council being present as a witness; 2, that a committee be appointed consisting of J. Pemberton, Alderman Pierpoint, Climcillors Lord, Forshaw, J. Roberts,and Barton, to inquire into the very Large amount of extras on the ' Delph-lane contract, the reason of same, and report findings to the Town Council. In moving the first resolution Councillor PemeeeroN said that his reason for doing so was the extraordinary expenditure on the waterworks undertaking. The con- tract was let for £24,000 and everybody thought it would be completed in the ordinary way. It was I thought there mteht be a little extra expenditure but that it would not extend to the thousands of pounds it ! had done. Although he was a member of the Water Committee, he did not know what the extras were. He had not seen the original contract or the specifications, though he had asked to see them as a member lof the Council. He had also applied to see the bill sent in by the contractor, with the extras, but his request was not acceeded to. The information had not been brought in an official way before the committee although the contract was finished some time ago. That, he contended, was a very improper way of con- ducting public improvements. Not only was he per- sonally refused the information once, but on another occasion he was accompanied by another Cofincillor as witness, and was not allowed to see the papers. If everything was straightforward there could be no reason for refusing permission to see the contracts, extras, and bills of quantities. If he gave figures which might not be correct, it would not be his fault bit the fault of the officials for not giving him the information he was entitled to. He had, however, good reason for stating that the cott of the work instead of bting .C 21.000 was likely to be nearer £50,000. That was a very serious item indeed. Councillor CLEGG : Are those your figures ? Councillor Pemuercrox : I have reason to believe the total cost may be that. Of course, the figures may , not be quite accurate. The Ma von : I think it is bad taste, considering I the way the thing is going on, for you to bring this up !before the proper time. I cannot see why you are doing it, whether it is in the public interest, or your private Interest, or what it is. I Councillor PEMBER.TON say that as a member of the Council and of the Water Committee, I was entitled 'in the public interest to see these papers, so that if there was anything which was not proper, I could have put my finger on it and brought the matter before the Council. If the business of tne Committee is going to degenerate into such a state as this, none of the coun- cillors will have any need to come here. You might as well leave it to the officials and the chairman of the Committee. No extra has a richt to be incurred with- out the consent of the Committee. After further argument dvith the Mayor;Councillor Pemberton said be could not understand why there should be so much secrecy about the matter. E%:ery member of the Council had a right to know what was going on. For two years he had been dissatisfied about this contract,and he had been told before Local Govern- ment Board inspectors that he was telling an untruth when he said he could not get information.. The Local Government Board inspectors were sent here to safe- guard the public interest and for any official to get up and tell a member of the Council that he was stating a deliberate untruth was a very serious accusation. _ _

The MAYOR.: Do you want to say we are wasting money and that the rest of the Council don't under- stand business, or do you want to know for your own private information? Councillor PENIBERTON : I don't want it for private information. I am not a well-sinker. Tae members of the Council have no more idea of this expenditure than a Hottentot. Continuing, he said that .at a previous meeting Alderman Francomh said no legal proceedings had been commenced and there were not likely to be any. On another occasion, however, he distinctly said that the reason why he (Councillor Pe:uberton) was not allowed to see the bills of quantities, specifications, Was because that there were likely to be legal proceed- ings between the Corporation and the contractor. Alderman FRANCOMB : That is not true.
The MAYOR : You never came and asked me when you wanted these papers._ You have been going behind the chairmen of committees.

The Tows CLERIC The papers were placed in my hands last week and I am engaged in examining them. I have gone through the papers and conferred with Mr. Lawson and Mr. Deas, and a report will be submitted to the committee with the accounts. If you pass this resolution T shall decline to accept any rosponsibility in connection with the contract.

Councillor PS.MBERTON : If the Council agrees to that it means that any contractor can enter into a con- tract with the Corporation and that no member of the committee can have access to documents or have any check upon the work as it proceeds. The MAYOR : You have the ordinary facilities of every member of the Council. You want extraordinary facilities for so•ne particular purpose. Councillor PENIBEnToN : You have no business to make such an accusation.

The INlAvort : Well, I say so. Councillor PEMBERTON : What object can I have in getting the information? You have no right to make the accusation unless you can prove it. When I wanted the information the job was completed. The MAYOR : It is not completed yet. It is under dispute now. Councillor PEMBERTON: The contract is completed The MAvoR: That Investigation Committee has cost the Corporation £25 already. It is in reference to two people and one case is practically connected with this matter. Why should you ask to see the papers while this is under dispute? You might wait until the case is settled.

Councillor PIMBERTON: It is a very proper thing for me to do. I am here in the public interest aud I say every Town oouncillor- -I:4The MAY-on :If the Council choose to hear you they can. lam inclined to leave the chair. _
Councillor PEMBERTON: Every Councillor ouiht to have free access to the papers. The MAYon: Reasonable access.

Councillor isntnmyroN : He ought to have access to every paper. If the thing is straightforward there is I no reason why he should not, and he ought not to have any unpleasantness. There are Councillors in this room who cannot get information but they dont persist because they don't want to be insulted. The Mavoa : They can't insult you. Councillor PEMBERTOA : No. lain here in the public interest and will do the best I can. It is an unpleasant job, one that I don't seek, and I should be glad to be out of it. It is very unpleasant and if everything was honest and straightforward there would be no need for it. (Loud "Hear, hears" from the public assembled at the back of the room). The Mayoa: If I have any more expressions from behind I will clear the lot of you out. If you can't behave yourselves you must go. This threat occasioned some further interruption. The MAYOR: Send a policeman. Police Sergeant Dean, the mace bearer, was sent for but when he appeared on the scene quietness had been restored, and no one was ejected. Councillor PEMBP:RTON resuming his speech, said the unpleasantness experienced deterred many gentlemen from making inquiries which they were entitled to make. The right to inspect the papers was really given to him (Councillor Pemberton) by law, but he did not think he ought to take action and spend his money. He asked the Town Council to pass the resolution on principle. Councillor LORD seconded. He thought Councillor Pemberton had very just cause for introducing She resolution. It was a scandalous state of affairs if the chairman of a committee and an official could defy a member of that committee. The MAYOR : Have you applied for whit Councillor Pemberton has asked for and been refused? Countillor LORI) : I am not going to answer any questions. They ire not on the agenda. (Laughter.) It is a scandalous state of affairs if a member of the Council cannot go into the details of the spending of £50,000, let alone a member of the committee. This state of thinas wants altering. Councillor JAMES EVANS said that according to Coun- cillor Pemberton the contract had been let at £24,000 and that extras amounting to .c2G,000 had been incurred, The TOWN CLERIC : The figures are not correct. Councillor EVANS said that if Councillor Pemberton's statement was anything like true and he had all along been a member of the committee which had had the work in hand, dhy on earth should not Councillor Pemberton, as well as any other member of the com- mittee, know what the extras were? If legal difficulties were pending, he took it that the committee would eventually be the body to deal with the bills of extras. The TOWN CLERIC: Of course they will. Councillor EVANS said that in that event the Council would have an opportunity of knowing all about the extras, and be thought Councillor Pemberton ought to wait, like he (Councillor Evans) was prepared to wait, until the committee had gone through its work. If it was found that there was anything like £26,000 in extras he (Councillor Evans) would want a great deal of detail about the spending of the money. He had never gone to seek reason- able information and been refused, and it was rather remarkable that the refusal of information should

apply only to Councillor Pemberton. It was calculated to create suspicion in the mind of the man who was outside the Council as well as of the member. They did not want any distrust creating in the town. There had been quite enough. There should be no trying to hide any legitimate infortnation that belonged to any member of the Council. He did not know whether it was within the power of the Corporation to supply Councillor Pemberton with the bill of quantities. Was it not absolutely the property of the contractor ? The TOWN Cum:: : Not absolutely. But he objects to its being disclosed at present. It is usual not to dis- close it until the contract is settled. Councillor PEMBERTON : Under the contract the contractor is bound to serve the Corporation with a copy of the bill of quantities. The Nlasou : lum informed that the contract is under seal until the matter is finished.

Alderman FRANCOMB said that what he objected to in Councillor Pemberton's speech was that he did not tell all truth. , His statement was partly true, but a lot was not true. For instance, he said the hill was com- pleted long ago, whereas it was only finished about May 12th. Again he said the contract was for £24,009 and that everyone thought the work was going to be done for £24,009. That was not at all correct. At every meeting of the Water Committee the whole thing was put down—what the contract was for,and how much each certificate was for—and it was there for everyone to see. This was a peculiar contract and other men besides Lawson tendered. The position was that if they got a certain quantity of water from the wells, there would be;nolextras for pumping,but if.they got above that amount they would have t ) pay for every additional 1,000 gallons pumped. The greatest water engineer they could consult told them they would get about a million and a quarter gallons per day, but instead of that they got four million gallons. The contractor could not, in fact, get pumps strong enough to cope with the supply and there were continual breakdowns. Every thousand gallons they pumped above a certain quantity meant extra expenditure above the .£24,000. When they con- sidered that they had those enormous wells, a mile-and- a-half in the ground, and that men had to work in them, surely they would not for the sake of a money matter allow the men to be drowned? As for stopping, it was an utter impossibility. If the work cost £50,000 it was a God-send to the town of IVarrington to have the extra I water. As to the miserable business, the suggestion that someone had been robbing the Corporation, he could not make it out. It seemed as if members of the Coun- cil came there to b 3 insulted and abused for their work. They had not even received the last bill from Lawson. The latest account sent in was marked " with reserva- tions." Must they without considering it, without allowing the Town Clerk and Water Engineer to examine the bill, rush and pay whatever the man asked them? Councillor Pemberton asked the other week whether there was any "law business'. in connec- tion with the contract. There was no law, and he did not know that they had any law even threatened now. He did not see any reason why they should not meet and 'make up their differences, but when it came to a great amount of extras—and necessary extras—he thought that they ware bound to agree that there must be differences of opinion, and that was going on at the present time. The bill as they received it was in the hands of the Town Clerk, and as soon as he was pre- pared to hand it over to the committee it would be brought before them. It almost amounted to a public scandal for Councillor Pemberton to be always saying that be could get no information. (Councillor Pember- ton : (Hear, hear.) He was in the habit of coming I when the business was over—

Councillor PEMBERTON : That is not true. Alderman FRXNCOMB: You were twenty minutes late one day and ten minutes another. If you do your work in that way yoi are sure to miss something. We are very satisffed with the result of our work out at Winwick, and I hope we shall have no quarrel whatever with the contractor. I sin hopeful that the Town Clerk will be able to reduce a large amount of extras to a very small one, and if that is so, I fancy the Cor- poration will he perfectly satisfied. Councillor MaGroz said he did not agree with the way in which Councillor Pemberton's arguments had been received that night. If there was any belief that Councillor Pemberton wanted the information for an ulterior or dishonest motive, he should be told plainly and straightforwardly: "We refuse to give you the information because we doubt the object for which you want it." If they were not prepared to say that, he held that every man elected to the Town Council by the rate- payers was entitled to conduct the business of the Council to the best of his ability, if he conducted it honestly. He could not agree with the chair- man of the Water Committee because he originally stated that he did not think it was wise to give Councillor Peinherton the information, as it was probable that the would have legal trouble. He (Coun- cillor Maginn) would never have given that unswer, but he would have stated the reason plainly. Councillor Evans said he would be content to argils the matter when the completed accounts came before them, but that would be a bit too late. The contract was let for £24,000, but he believed there was an enormous sum for extras—although it was contradicted that the extras were £2WIOO. How much had already been paid in extras ?
jThe Towx CLERK : There are no' extras at all. Councillor Maotxx : Then we have only paid £21,001 The TOWN CLERS : We have paid according to con- tract for work done.
Councillor 11aGINS: That argument may snit you, but—

The MAYOR: You don't nnderstand what he means. The contract was let for £24,000 but contingencies might arise that would make it impossible to carry it out on the lines laid down—such as excess of water,—and be was to be paid extra for pun4ping all the water above a certain quantity. Councillor MAGI-NY If the contract provides for certain money to be paid under certain conditions wAI and good, bet if there are conditions which give him the power to alter the accounts every time be likes then it is no contract at all.

.... The MAYOR.: The contract was made by the old Water Committee. Since then the constitution of the committee has changed but the present committee has to carry out the terms of the contract. Alderman FRANCO:MIR explained that the contract was let for £24,000 but the Corporation had to pay for every thousand gallons of water pumped over a certain quantity. That had resulted in complicating matters and at the present time the Town Clerk and the Water Engineer were trying to unravel them. It was quite possible that many of the extnis would be objected to. At the same time it would not do for them to give themselves away when there was a chance of settling them. in a little more time they would have all the figures which they required.._ •

naousx: I object to thst. Is it right that you should come to this Council with a bill after you have settled it? The NTAYOR: The contract was accepted and carried out according to the details of every contract of every committee of the Corporation. I think there is some- thing wrong and I don't know the meaning of it. Councillor Mac:N:4 : It certainly looks very bad and if Councillor Pemberton has no reason for this, save to make the Water Committee look radiations and to show the man.gement of the town's bnsiness. I pity him. The contract is let for £21,000 and we have already paid £37.000 and it is public property that we have still £lO,OOO to`pay. I think it would have been better if the Water Committee had taken the whole Council into their confidence. The extras have beeh so excessive that, with all due respect to the Town Clerk and the Water Engineer, I say it is too mucii for them to take upon themselves to settle the accounts. itly question has not been answered. I asked how much we I have already paid in entries. I do not think it fair that the Town Clerk should threaten the Council.
The IVIA.yon : You misunderstand him. He says that as a lawyer he will not take the responsibility for the account If someone else is allowed to interfere with

The TOWN CLERK : If you pass this resolution and allow Councillor Pemberton and others to see these papers before we have settled with Lawson I will not accept the responsibility. Councillor Maorss : If this extra money has been spent it would have been better if the Water Committee had taken the Council into their confidence. The Tows Cr.knx : The amount paid to Lawson is .4.-'31,48-1. 1 repeat there are no extras in that sum. Councillor Macitss : There is £ll,OOO spent more than the amount of the contract.
The MAYOR : The contract was for £21,000, subject to certain conditions.

Alderman FRANCOMB : We could not stop the water coming in. Councillor MAGINN : Could' you not say to the Council, " We have had to pay this money " ? Alderman FRANCOMB: Ile Council has agreed to the payment. There is no hiding at all and there never has been. Councillor BARTON : After what has been said in the past I was hoping these differences were dead and buried and have been thinking that if any information is to be given it should not be given to Councillor Pemberton but to the whole of the Council. • Councillor PEMBERTON: "Hear, hear."

_ The ATAVOR: Councillor Pemberton eau depend upon it the Town Council will not pay one penny more than they can help. Councillor BurtTox : It seems to me that instead of a committee being appointed it would be better to call in an independent expert who will thoroughly under- stand the whole business.

The MAYOR : You have appointed your arbitrator accoccling to the contract. Mr. DEAS explained that be had not had a final account from Lawson. The account which had been sent in was with reservations.

The AI Axoa: We are showing our hands. Some members of the Council think there are a lot of honest men except in this Council Chamber and we have to have committees of inquiry. It is not addini to the dignity of the Council to have these things going on. Councillor LORD: The committees are necessary. Councillor Burtros : I take it that anything which is right, proper and legal can be seen at any time by the members of the Council. Alderman FRANCOMB: I have never withheld any- thing. Councillor Pemberton came one holiday and wanted some information. lie wanted to keep the clerks working. Councillor PEMBERTON : And you refused to give me the papers. Alderman Fa.s.xcamu Of course I efused you.

Yo 3 cannot keep the clerks working on a bank holiday. Councillor PmraErtras7 : It 'vs not a bank holiday. Councillor SroCT : I was of the opinion that every member of the Cannon should have the same facilities for seeing any documents they wish to see as any mem- ber of the committee.

_ Alderman Fitascoms : So they have. Toe Nlayort : There are some documents you cannot expose. Om came to me the °that. day which it would not do for every member of the Council to see. Councillor LORD: Was it with regard to the business of the Council?

The favott : YO9. It WAR a matter of buying and selling land. I could not allow any member of the Corporation to go through it. Councillor PEMBERT3N: We are not to be trusted. Councillor STOTT: Councillor Pemberton has not given any satisfactory instance of any paper or contract which he has asked to sae being refused. Nothing has ever been refused me. It would be well if the Council could satisfy Councillor Pemberton. The 31avon : I asked him for what interest he requires tp see the documents. Councillor PENlcErtrox : In the public interests. Councillor STOTT : The point is whether a member of the Council shall give you his reason for wanting to see certain documents. The NIA Yon : You put me at the Gad of affairs to deal on your behalf. and if anything is required out of the ordinary way I expect to be treated with that courtesy. If asked for what is required I can give a proper answer. Councillor STOTT : COOnCillOr PoMbertOrl has from time to time asked for information and has been refused. The MAYOR : Ile has never asked me. C.ouncillor STOTT : He has asked the Chairman of the Water Committee and the Water Engineer.

An inquest was held at Warrington, on Wednesday, on the body of Annie Whitfield (33), of Winsford- street, who was found dead in bed after having taken a dose of carbolic acid. Deceased was a married woman, lout had lived apart from her husband for eight years. She often said idle wished she were dead, and was stranize in her mini. Oa Saturday she plisoned herself while] in drink. A verdict of "Suicide while of unsound mind " was returned.

We regret to announce the death which took place at hi 4 residence 9, Marsh House-lane, on Tuesday, of Mr. John H. Scarisbrick, one of the assistant school attendance inspectors in the employ of the Warring- ton Education Comtnittee. Mr. Scartsbrick had been in indifferent health for some time, suffering from cardiac affection. The deceased gentleman had faith- fully served the community in the capacity of school attendance inspector for about ten years. His devotion to duty, and his unvarying courtesy in its discharge, earned for him the respect of all those with whoin he came into contact, being very highly esteemed by his ' colleagues. ! H. M. Aldermsn FRINCOMB: He hits never 'been refused.

Councillor STOTT : Has Councillor Pemberton made application to see these documents except on that special day? Councillor MA.GINS: Was he refused on account of the day? Alderman FnA:scomn: Yes. It was only by chance that I was at the water works. After consulting with Mr. Dols, Alderman FRANCO:UR said that no member of the cournittee had seen the con- ditions of contract.

COUBCiIIOr PEMBERTON: It is a great shame. Alderman FRANCOMB said the reason he objected to give Conncillor Pemberton the information when he called at the office was because it would keep the clerk's waiting there when everyone had a holiday. Councillor PEMBERTON: You did not give that reason than.

Alderman FRANCOMTI: You knew it was the reason. It is perfect nonsense to talk like that. Councillor PENIIIErtTON said he wrote giJing Mr. Dens notice that he would call at the office on a certain day. He went at eleven o'clock in the morning—it was not a Bank Holiday—and his request was refused. Later he called in company with Councillor Horrocks and when he asked Mr. Haas to be allowed to see the papers, he replied "No. r have the authority of Mr. Fra.ncomb for not showing them." Alderman FFLANCOnB: Mr. Deas says you did not write to him. Besides that, do you think that as chair- man of the committee I would over-ride the members of the committee and give information of this kind without getting their permission? I would not do it for anyone. Councillor Pemberton did not turn up on Saturday as he promised. , Co:mentor PFABERTON:_ How do you know that?

Alderman Pri.A.Ncomn : I have it down here. Monchy was a holiday and ths office wis closed. Mr. D3as was there from 9.30 to 11.33 and Mr. Pemberton was not at the office daring those hours.oa Tuesday Mr.Peaoerton called at 11.15. _ . _
Councillor STOTT : VVas the chairmln or the Com- mittee willinz to show Mr. Pemberton the docoments?

Alderman FRINCOMB : I had not the authority. Councillor Srorr : I want to know whether Nan- cillor Pemberton has a right as a member of the Council to sea the documents. If he has not aright to see them we ought to have some explanation why. The 111Avort : He has a right to ask at any committee meeting for any documents to be brought up if that committee decides that they shall be produced. Councillor STOTT said that if there was any chance of satisfying Councillor Pemberton and disproving his allegations, he would agree to such steps being taken. The MAYOR. : There is no t!ossible chance of satisfy- ing some members of the Council. .

• - The Tows CLERK: I would like to emphasise certain remarks (Mate Sfavor. Mr. Lawson has made a serious allegation against Councillor Pemberton and I think it. is inadvisable to pass the motion in its present form until the allegation is proved or disproved. Councillor BENSON supported the proposition. Councillor PEMBERTON, in replying to the criticisms. sail he wanted to see the specifications, contract and plant because ho received certain serious information. With the object of ascertaining the true state of affairs, he intended to go down the wells in company with Councillor Lord to inspect the work. Fie knew that there were 300 yards to be driven and that the Council were being charged for more, and he claimed the right to measure it for himself. He was, however. kept out of the wells until the water had been turned in. and now the measurement could never be taken. If there was any man on that Council to whom it would not be safe to show letters and documents, he ought to be hounded out as a dishonest man.
The MAYOR: Is there any hair on the palm of you hand ? (Laughter). Councilor PEMBERTON : Yes.

The NIATOR : lam glad to know it. You are the first honest man I have seen. Councillor PEMBERTON : There are no other honest men in the Council, then? Councillor LORD : Ttrit is an insult to the rest of the Coun,il. _ .

Councillor PENIEFATON : Every man has his price hut no man has reached my price yet. Because I fight for whit is straightforward and honest, I era insulted in this way. Continuing Councillor Pemberton said the contract stated that Mr. Lawson should pro- vide plant to pump three million gallons a day. If he pumped over that quantity the Council had to nay him for the extra plant. There had been no checking of the quality, except by Mr. Deas and an assistant.. If he (Councillor Pemberton) thought it was in the interests of the ratepayers hs had a right to go and check it. In his opinion the Council was being hood- winked. It was untrue that he called at the water engineer's office on a Bank Holiday, for there was a meeting of the Council the same evening. The contract WAS not sealed up. The Mayon: The bill of quantities is sealed up, Councillor PEuitcaTov‘; Then how can you check the bill? Continuing ho said that by pure accident one of Mr. Lawson's bills was sent to the committee, and that was the only one be (Councillor Pemberton) had seen during the %hole of the time he had served on the committee. There was an amount of 1:303 for driving an adit and oernenting it—that was for 26 days—and for 26 days extra pumping they paid Mr. Lawson £lloo.That was on £3OO worth of work. That was the reason ho wanted to see the details. _ _

...... The ALIYOR: And you allowed the committee to pass it. Councillor P. EmsEaroN: T objected to it strongly. But what was the use ? —There is not a :zingle man on the Water Committee who tholoughly understands the business.

The Itlxvon : This is all done for the benefit of the public—to obtain notoriety. The resolution was then put to the vote but as only Councillors Lord, Benson and Pemberton voted for it, it was defeated.
The second resolution met with a similar fate, Coun- cillor John Roberts having previously declined to serve on the sub-committee.

STRUGGLE FOR A RAZOR. At the Borough Police Court on Wednesday Peter MacDonough was charged with attempting to commit suicide by cutting his throat with a razor, in the dwell- ing-house of 29, Rose and Crown-street, on Tuesday afternoon. Superintendent Monaghan said prisoner was lodging at the house. He was a labourer, and had been drinking heavily for the last fortnight. On Tuesday afternoon he was seen by a woman named Clarke to take the razor from a rack in the back kitchen and draw it across his throat. After a struggle Mrs. Clare succeeded in taking the razor from him.—Prisouer was remanded for a week.

div.p: WARRINGTON TOWN COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of the Town Council was held on Tuesday when there were present :—The Mayor (Alderman Bolton), Alderman A. Bennett, John Evans, R. W. Francomb, D. Tinnion, Councillors T. Barton, W. Benson, W. Brough, T. Burton, NV. Clegg, James Evans, L. Ellison, W. J. Forshaw, Dr. Joseph, J. Lord, J. Maginn, A. Peacock, P. Peacock, J. Pemberton, J. Roberts, J. Sankey, J. Skelland, J. F. Smith, F. Stott, W. J. Wilson, T. Wright, Messrs. J. L. Whittle (Town Clerk), 'F. A. Hallaway (Deputy 'fown Clerk), J. Fair- hurst (Borough Treasurer), T. Longdin (Borough Surveyor). J. Deas (Water Engineer), F. V. L. Matthias (Electrical Engineer), J. G. Gornall (Medical Officer), J. M. Murray (Director of Education). THE HOUSING OF THE WORKING-CLASSES. At a meeting of the Finance and Estate Committee an application received from the tenant of No. 66, West- street, for an advance under the small dwellings acquisi- tion act, 1899, in order to enable him to purchase the house, was considered, and the Town Clerk was instructed to make preliminary inquiries into the matter. At a later meeting the Town Clerk submitted the result of his inquiries and the Borough Surveyor was instructed to report fully upon the value of the premises. The minutes of the Committee were approved. THE PURCHASE OF LAND.

The Street Improvement and Lightity, Committee recommended that the sum of £637 G. BS. be paid to Messrs. Greenall, Whitley and Co., Ltd., as compensa- tion for setting back the line of frontage in School Brow opposite the Bricktnakers Arms. Councillor STOTT thought the price to be paid was very high indeed, especially after the concessions which had from time to time been made to the vendors. The MAYOR explained that Messrs. Greensll, Whitley and Co., were asking the price which the land had cost them.

The minntes were approved. NEW BACTERIA BEDS AT LONGFORD. At a meeting of the Sanitary Works Committee the engineer reported upon and submitted estimates for the constriction of five additional bacteria beds at long- ford Depot, at an estimated cost of £1,200. It was resolved that the same be approved, and that the Town Clerk be authorised to apply to the Local Government Board for the necessary borrowing powers. It was further resolved, that the works be carried out by the corporation workmen uuder the supervision of the engineer. • Alderman EVAlcs in moving the adoption of the minutes explained that an experimental bacteria had been in existence at Longford for some time and had done very satisfactory work. The construction of the new beds would be a big advantage and would help to improve the stream into which the effluence from the works was discharged. With reference to the decision ' to carry out the work themselves they felt that the work would be more carefully done under the direction

but he was going to take complete control of a library. The speaker thought that the flavour of the compliments which had been paid Mr. Howarth was rather spoiled by having coupled with them a sort of back-handed slap at Mr. Madeley. ..,:.Councillor PEMBERTON: I protest against that remark. If I had anything to say against Mr. Madeley I should say it outright and not gives back-handed slap. Alderman BENNETT: The discussion seems to have that colour. Councillor PEMBERTON: It has not. ..

Alderman BENNETT coutinuinr, said he was pleased to hear Councillor Pemberton valued Mr.Madeley's services. The whole cause of the trouble lay in the fact that they were limited to the lid, rate for library purposes. The same difficulty would crop up over the pictures he hoped they were going to buy. (Laughter.) That was why they could not see their way to pay salaries to officials. The remuneration they paid their officers 1151 really disgraceful, but they had only a limited income, and it was impossible to be more generous until they had a larger revenue. He repudiated most strongly the assertion that the library was in a hopeless state, was in fact a pre-historic ante- deluvian sort of library and was not in any sense up to the requirements of the 2Jth century. The library got as much spent upon it as it was entitled to and the refer- ence library was a very admirable one indeed and one of which they had every reason to be proud. The minutes were approved. BIRDS LOST FROM THE AVIARY. In moving the confirmation of the minutes of the Town Hall Park and Baths Committee the Mayor said that the bowling green which had been opened in Victoria Park was very satisfactory and appeared to be very much appreciated. CouncAlor ELLISON seconded. Alderman TINNION asked if it was true that birds had been lost out of the aviary. The TOWN CLERK: Nearly all. The MAYOR : We gave out a contract for a new top to be put on. As usual we like to see that we get value for our money and we let the top wear out before we put another on. (Laughter.) Councillor WRIGHT asked if the bowls in use were those referred to in the minutes ? The MAYOR : Oh, yes. They are now in use. Councillor WitiGHT : Is it according to the Stand- ing Orders that articles or materials shall bo bought and put into use before they are sanctioned by the Council ?
The MAvou : Yes the expenditure is under £2O so it was unnecessary to advertise. The minutes were confirmed. COUNCILLOR J. ROBERTS AND THE BIRTH OF

ADAM. TO "DO AWAY" WITFI ONE MAN. A !fleeting of the Markets Committee was held on June 5, when the following resolution was passed "That Messrs. G. T. Rushton and Harold Brizell be nominated to sit for the examination of Weights and Measures Inspectors."—The Borough Surveyor reported that he had obtained tenders for a sandblast machine, and that the cost would he from £l5 to £5O. It was resolved that the Borough Surveyor be authorized to proceed with the work, and also flag a portion of the Fish Market to the end of the stalls.—At another meet- ing on the 19th June, it was resolved that Mr. Percy 0. Bailey be nominated to sit for the examination of Weights and Measures Inspector. Councillor RonEnTs moved the conflrmation of the minutes, and alluded at length to the minute with refer- ence to the sandblast machine. The old machine had, he said, been in use since the birth nf Adam.
Alderman TINNION : Adam was not born. (Laughter). Alderman FRANCOMB : Was he not made out of a rib ?

Alderman TINNION : He was not made out of a rib. , (More laughter.) ! Councillor ROBERTS (continuing), said the new machine would be fully capable of doing away with one man. (Laugher.) He meant that it would do away with the services of one man, but not that it would do away with the man. The minutes were approved. THE WATER SUPPLY. • IMPROVEMENTS TO THE ENGINE AT WIINWICK. At a meeting of the Water Committee, on June sth, it was resolved that the tender of Messrs. James Simp- son and Son, Ltd., of London, for compounding the beam engine at Winwick Pumping Station at £1,530 be accepted; and that the Town Clerk apply to the Local Government Board for their sanction to the borrowing of the sum of £1,600 for the above purpose. Alderman FRANCOMB, in moving the confirmation of the minutes, submitted the following statement;—At a meeting held 15th August, 1901, it was resolved that the Engineer be instructed to prepare a specification in order to obtain tenders for the repairing of the old engine at Winwick Pumping Station. At the following meeting, 29th August. 1901, it was resolved that Alder- man Evans and Councillor Duncan be appointed a sub- committee to confer with the Engineer in the preparation of a specification for the repair- ing of the old engine at Winwick Pumping Station, in consequence of shortage of power. The matter lay somewhat in abeyance until the 17th April, j 1905, when the Engineer reported on the compounding lof the old engine, and at was resolved that he be instructed to prepare specifications and obtain tenders for the work. Specifications were prepared and the work was advertised on April 28th. On 22nd May, 1905, the tenders were placed before the Water Committee, were opened and referred to , Alderman Evans and Mr. Dells to report thereon. This :report was considered by the Water Committee at the meeting held sth June and they resolved to accept Messrs. Simpson and Co.'s tender. While the cost of the work is £l,OOO it must be remembered that this includes both compounding and repairing. The cost might probably be apportioned £l,OOO for compounding and ..£6OO for repairine. It is confidently expected that Ithe higher duty will ensure a saving in fuel amounting to £2 per week, so that it will be seen that this will cover interest and sinking fund. The engine will be completely dismantled and rebuilt, and so will be practi- cally a new engine. It must be remembered that at the present time it is impossible to work this engine owing to want of repairs, and so we have no stand-by at Win- wick with the exception of a small horizontal engine. If any breakdown, necessitating a stoppage of more than two days, took place at Houghton Green at the present time we should not bo able to supply the pre- sent demand with the present available plant at Winwick. Alderman Francomb added that Mr. Deas had prepared a report on the subject. Councillor PEMBERTON Said he thought it would be better to leave the compounding of the engine over for the present. The matter had been a bit hurried. The engine was only going to be a stand-by, and it would be better to repair it and leave it as is simple engine, and not compound it. He would not spend the extra £l,OOO. ,He did not think it was worth it. The saving could not be so great as was stated when the engine was only being used as a stand-by. There was no doubt .that at Delph-lane the Council would in the near future be asked to sanction another engine. It was wrong to bring into the discussion any shortage of water as it did not apply. He would ask the Chairm.n of the Water Committee to withdraw the matter so that it might be considered again. Councillor Nine:lNN said they were told they were lifting sufficient water from Delp'n-lane to supply the town when there were 200,000 of a population. Alderman FR.A.NCOMB : Not lifting, but that we had the water there if we required it. (Hear, hear.) The Mivort : It is only like having an insurance, and you are insuring yourself from an accident. You want to take time by the forelock and put the machinery n good order while you can. Councillor EVANS said they were told they would have to provide a new engine at Delph-lane. Would the engine at Winwick if put in repair, serve the purpose apart from the consideration of saving? Alderman EVANS: For a time, yes. Councillor EVANS thought the best thing after all was to'pet the engine in repair. If it was only to be used as a stand-by it was not worth spending £1,600 on it.
Councillor PEMBERTON moved, as nn amendment, that the engine be put in order, but that it need not be com- pounded. The MAYOR : You cannot put it that way..

COUneillOC LORD moved an amendment to the effect that the minute referring to the engine be referred back to the committee for father consideration. He said he thought it was a waste of money to spend £1,600 on the old engine. Cenncillor IhnTos seconded the amendment. Alderman TENSION was in favour of putting the engine in thorough order. Alderman EVANS denied that the engine was worn out. It was a type that was acknowledged to be most economical, and all was good about it except the gear- ing and the crank shaft. Councillor INlnorNsr asked what the engine would be worth when compounded and £1,600 was spent on it. There was no reply. Alderman TINNION : What would a new one cost?
Councillor MAGINN thought it would be cheaper to have a new engine in the circumstances.

Alderman EVANS observed that the one at Delph-lane cost £ll,OOO. Its capacity was three million gallons in 24 hours, so he thought it would be fair to estimate the the value of the Winwick engine when put in order at one third of that amount. Councillor MAGINN: IS it still proposed to carry on the Winwick pumping statian no matter what we spend on Delph-lane? The Mayon: The water is quite as good ; better, in fact, than the other. The committee will never allow anything to slip out that is good. Two strings to the bow are better than one. Two wells are better than one one might grow dry. (Hear, hear, and laughter.) Comicillor PEMBERTON supported the amendment. He did not say the engine should not be put in repair. It would pay the Corporation to put it in repair, and work it the way it was worked for 30 years, but it would not pay the ratepayers to spend an extra thousand pounds on it.No one thought of it except as a stand-by engine; to compare it with the Delph-lane engine was simply a farce. Councillor BURTON thought sufficient explanation had not been given to warrant the Council in supporting the minutes of the committee. Councillor STo-rr was of the same opinion ; more information ought to be given; not that he objected to th compounding if it was shown to be necessary. Alderman FRANCOME said he was not a engineer. He was simply the mouthpiece of the committee, but he contended that with such men to advise as Alderman Evans, Councillor Duncan, and Mr. Deas to guide them in the right way, they need have no fear about the supply of water. (Hear, hear.) They had now an abundance of water at both places, especially at Delph- lane, indeed the supply seemed unlimited. If they mad, a good job of the engine it would help to stave off the time when they might have to put another engine down at Delph-lane. He thought it was the duty of the Council to put the engine iu proper repair. (Hear, hear.) The matter had been on the carpet two years, even before the new boilers were put in, and consider- able time and care had been spent in discussing the matter. lie had every confidence in the opinion of Alderman Evans, the engineer, and Councillor Duncan. The voting resulted as follows FOR THE AMENDMENT. AG k INST. Councillor Evans Alderman Francomb tt 7t Barton Bennett Pt Skelland Tinnion Lord Evans Burton Councillors Roberts Dr. Joseph Fulton Smith Maginn Pt Clegg llenson Wi I son ' Pemberton Sankey PP ), Stott A. Peacock PP Wright P. Peacock Brough-12 tf Wilson and the Mayor-13 The MAYOR : The amendment is lost. The minutes were then agreed to in their entirety. PHYSICAL INSTRUCTION FOR SCHOOL CHILDREN. EDUCATION COMMITTEE AS "GRAND- MOTHERS." The Gymnasium Committee reported that the Town Clerk laid before the committee a return of replies received from other towns in reference to the instruc- tion of school children in physical drill, from which it appeared thnt the instruction was carried out under the sup3rvision of or by the g7/mastic instructor in eight towns out of ten replies received. It was resolved that the School Management Committee be informed that in the opinion of this committee the scheme originally agreed to and confirmed by the Council would be the most satisfactory and to the best interests of the school children, and with that object in view this committee cannot agree to any scheme which does not provide for the co-operation and assistance of this committee and its officers. Alderman TINNION moved the approval of the minutes and said he hoped the Council would support them in the stand they had taken. Judging from tne feeling expressed by Canon Morley Stevenson, he thought it was probable that some arrangement might be come to, and that the School Management Committee would see that it was utterly preposterous and ridiculous for them to expect the Gymnasium Committee to put the Gymna- sium into their hends from nine o'clock on the Monday morning until noon on Saturday, without having some- thing to say rte to the kind of instruction to be given to the children. It seemed to be the idea that the Gymna- sium Committee wished to give the children instruction in gymnastics. They wanted to do nothing of the kind, but wished to give the proper physical instruction set forth by the Education Department. They held that they were the proper committee to give the drill, and see that it was given properly. They understood it quite as well as the teachers, members and chairman of the School Management Committee, and thought that efficiency would only be obtained by the co-operation of that committee and the Gymnasium Committee. Councillor SKELLAND seconded the approval of the minutes. Alderman BENETT said he did not think the Educa- tion Committee woeld see the matter in the same light as Alderman Tinnion. The Education Committee were responsible for the education of the children, and it was for them to say what they considered the best means of giving physical drill. It seemed as if there was a difference in principle between the committees which it would be impossible to bridge. The School Manage- ment Committee thought the teachers were fully qualified to give the instruction. The question of the use of the Gymnasium being allowed might be recon- sidered, but on the question of drill it was a matter for the Education Committee to decide. The stand the Gymnasium Committee took reminded one of the old adage "Don't try to teach your grandmother to suck eggs." (Laughter.) The MAYOR: That might apply the other way about. : Councillor EVANS said the point that most concerned him was whether the action of the Education Com- mittee in desiring to have this drill given by the teachers was the thin end of the wedge to pave the way for an appeal to the ratepayers for the provision of playgrounds or places indoors attached to the schools for the teaching of the drill. The Council ought to , know exactly how they stood before they ventured at all in that direction, because if the Education Committee , got permission to do the drilling themselves they miet next want places of their own to do it in. (Hear, hear.) I Councillor M A GINN said he understood the schools ' were carrying out the conditions laid down by the ' Board of Education. He thought it was nonsense for Alderman Tinnion to suggest that all the school children I oueht to go to the Gymnasium to be taught physical I drill. There had recently been complaints about taking children away from school for a short time for religious worship, and yet it was suggested that children should come from one end of the town to the other in order to have physical drill at the Gymnasium. The Council would always have the opportunity of opposing any ! scheme to providesepamte drilling places at theschools. Alderman TtatarfosT said it was almost impossible to correct some of the—he was going to say—crass ignor- ance of some of the members. He had never suggested for a moment teat they should take children from the far end of the town to the Gymnasium, nor had the suggestion ever been made. Ile was referring to the children attending the schools in the immediate neigh- bourhood of the Gymnasium and the pupils at the , Higher Grade School and Pupil Teachers' Centre. The j School Management Committee in they resolution they wisely withdrew, offered the Gymnasium Committee I £3O for the use of the Gymnasium for the children and I £2O a year if they would instruot teachers in physical I drill. .Aderrnan Bennett, he ventured to say, knew as much about this drill as a sweep did about a clean shirt. Alderman BENNETT : Is that in order, Mr. Mayor ? I don't think it is quite necessary for Alderman Tinnion to he offensive. Th 3 MAYOR : Well, you wars talking about grand mothers and sucking eggs and he is getting a bit of his own back. (Laughter). Alderman Ttststo's : Alderman Bennett said we (the Gymnasium Committee) wanted to teach our grand- mothersi ei en Well, I have had my own p sEudctkicea eggs. Committee, but I haveleft eabout thet o it to the Chairman of the Committee to say what he thinks about them. He evidently thinks they are grandmothers. (Laughter.) I don't quarrel with his opinion. I have had that opinion for some time, but I have not expressed it quite as boldly as that. (Laughter.) Continuing, he said the Education Department issued it syllabus with reference to physical drill which must he carried out. Physical instruction, in the eyes of the department, was as important as any other part of school worlc, and must be given efficiently. The School Management Committee said they had 169 teachers trained in physical drill, but not one of them had the drill in college because it was a new drill based on the Swedish drill. TRAM EXTENSION IN BRIDGE STREET. The Tramways Committee recommended that the tram lines in Bridge-street be extended front Rylands- street northwards at an estimated cost of £7OO, and that the Town Clerk apply to the Board of Trade for sanction to the borrowing of that amount. In the absence of the Chairman and Deputy-Chairman the MAYort moved the confirmation of the minutes. He

said it was necessary to pave Bridge-street where the widening had taken place, and they thought they might do two things at once by extending the tram-lines while doing the paving. It would be better to put the lines down now instead of proceeding with the paving and then having to take it up again to put down the lines later on. The Board of Trade Inspector had inspected the Stoc'iton Heath extension. There was a little trouble with the signals, but possibly the cars would be running next week. Alderman TiNNWN said the extension would facilitate the running of the cars from Rylands-street and there would no longer be the complaint that the cars could not be seen at the terminus by people coming along Bridge-street. There was a great wear and tear on the curve which would he obviated, but in any event the curve would have to be relayed and it would be advis- able to provide the new points now. The .£7OO would include the repairs to the curve.

Councillor EVANS moved that the minute be not con- firmed. He said that if they made the extension it would not be used for four or five years at least,so that their money would he "corroding ' away. The street would need repaving before the new line was used. Alderman TENNION : The extension will be used daily. The NTAvoix : The Paving and Sewerage Committee will have to pave this, and it we delay this extension it will mean taking the paving up again when it is done. Councillor P. PEACOCK objected to the Electricity Committee borrowing money to carry out repairs, and seconded the amendment on that ground.

Councillor 11.IaGINN said this 4.0,8 a very necessary expenditure. Besides the curve wearing out very quickly it was constantly injuring the trolleys, owing to the sharp bend. This extension would save the Wilderspool cars from that. Also, they should consider how ridicu- lous it was for trains to be blocking Bylands-street all the day through. It was absolutely necessary that the curve should be relaid, and in doing it now, and making the extension, they would be rAeving the strain on some of this cars and relieving the congestion at Itylands-street. Alderin TINNIONT said some members often talked about streets bola; paved and then taken up again by the framways Committee or the G.s Committee or somebody else, and now when they wanted to obviate that an amendment was moved. The Council would be wise in allowing the two committees to co-operate in ' this case and making the exten3ion. The street wanted paving at once, and they had already had a lawyer's letter from someone who had slipped on the pavement . A more unreasonable amendment had hardly ever been prolosod in the Council. Only the proper and seconder voted for the amend- ment, and the extension was approved by a large ! majority.

The General Purposes Committee reporteu they hadresolved that the Town Clerk negotiate with Messrs. Greenlll, Whitley and Company for the purchase of the Lied required for the widening of Warrington Bridge; and that the Town Clerk write to Admiral Sir George Nares. the Acting Conservator of the Mersey request- ing him to give his assent to the proposed alterations to the bridge. That was the result of the dissatisfaction expressed by certain members of the Council.

div.head: STANLEY'S MAGIC BOOK. 0 A TRUE STORY.
div.p: STANLEY'S MAGIC BOOK. 0 A TRUE STORY.

On the bank of an African river, upon a tiny clearing which—scooped out of the vast black forest that bristled along both shores as far ak the eye can reach—betokened the neighbourhood of a native village, a man was standing alone, taking rapid dotes in a small book, while behind him lay moored along the water's edge a fleet of canoes, crowded with the dark-brown or black faces of Arabs and negroes, whose crooked swords and long ivory-stocked guns glittered in the morning sunshine. The solitary figure on the bank seemed to be the only white man of the whole party, and even lean and ragged as he was, with his face burned almost black by the sun, and a matted mane of grayish black hair and beard hanging loosely around it, seemed quite as savage as any of his followers. But, small and thin though he was,with plain, almost coarse features, an a dress of which any respectable scarecrow would have been ashamed, he had in his sunken eyes that look of power and command which stamps the born leader of men. And such, indeed, he was, for-this man was no other than Henry Morton Stanley. So engrossed was Stanley with the notes which he was making, that he never saw the black scowling face and fierce eyes which peered out at him suddenly from the encircling thicket. Presently another head appeared, and another, and another still; and then the matted boughs shook and parted, and several men stole forth, with long spears in their hands. But Stanley's quick ear had caught the rustle of the leaves, and, taking several strings of beads from his pouch, he advanced to meet them, uttering the long, shrill, bleat-like salutation of the country, " Sen-nen-neh I" (peace). But there was little sign of peace among the advancing savages, who darted threatening looks at him, and kept muttering angrily among themselves. Then a huge scarred warrior, who seemed to be their chief, said, with a flourish of his spear: "If the white man wishes peace, why does he try to bewitch us?" 'How have I tried to bewitch you?" asked Stanley in amazement. " I come as your guest, not as your enemy. You all see that my men have laid down their guns and swords, and are 'waiting to be friends with you." (To be continued.)

THINGS WE SHOULD LIKE TO KNOW. Where did Old Mother Hubbard live? Which market did the five little Pigs go to? What was the size of the pie little Jack Horner put his thumb into? Where did Boy Blue buy his horn? Who soled and heeled Cinderella's slipper? Who made the Red Riding Hood? —4--- A MATTER OF TASTE. Says the peacock to the rabbit, "Who's your tailor? tell me, pray; For, good sir, he's cut your coat-tail In a most old-fashioned way. Look at me, Would you see What a stylish tail should be!" Says the rabbit to the peacock, "Who's your barber? tell me, pray; For his shears have Omni your ears, sir, In a most old-fashioned way. Look at me, Would you see What a stylish ear should be I"

div.p: THE ADVENTURE OF A WOODEN DUCK. Once upon a time I lived i with a lot of MY wooden relations in a beautiful coloured wooden house, called a Noah's Ark. But, after a time, L got tired of living the same life day after day, so I made up my mind to see the world.4llWell, the next time we were put on the table I tried to fall off, which performance I managed very success- fully, and I fell on the floor without my mistress missing me. The night came on, and all the toys were put away, and I remained where I had fallen unseen. I waited patiently till the clock struck twelve, for at that time you know, dear children, all we toys have an hour given to us in which we can walk and talk like human beings. At last the clock struck twelve, and at once I got up and started off to see what I could of the world. I wandered on for some time, and then, to my horror, I saw a large mouse coming to- wards me. I screamed at the top of my voice, and at that moment. fortunately for me, rcY little mistress's nurse, who slept in the saw° room, opened the door with a light in her hand* and, seeing a mouse, exclaimed, 'Dear rae; there's another of these horrid little things; , must have a trap put down," and flung a towet she had in her hand after the mouse. As she stooped to pick up the towel, she saw me lying. on the floor. "Dear me I one of Miss Mabel's best toys, too She is careless," and, picking To° up, she put me back in the Noah's Ark among my friends, and I assure you, my dear readers, I have never tried to wander again. alight away.)

div.head: About the Dukeries.
div.p: About the Dukeries.

The fame of the district known as the "Dukeries," considered as a touring-ground for cyclists, has spread far and wide.. Not only do the stately homes of We;beck and Clumber form an attraction, but the exceptionally beautiful wood- land scenery of Sherwood Forest is worth going far to see. London riders are not as favourably Placed as northerners for visiting the district, for Worksop, the most convenient starting-point, is 145 miles distant frau the metropolis. Some years ago, when the writer Cycled through the Dukeries on a tandem, it was by no means easy to obtain the necessary local information. New an excellent up-to-date guide, .11-beelmarki round Worksop,' may be had for lid. A complete tour of the Dukeries occupies a day, about 30 miles being covered, and can only be made on Mondays, Thursdays, and • Saturdays. A pass, presented gratis, must be applied for at the Newcastle Estate Office, Worksop, to admit to Clumber and Tboresby Park. After this formality has been observed all is plain sailing, whether the visitor ride a cycle or form one of a party driven in a char-a-bane. But, be it observed, the motorist on a petrol-propelled vehicle, is debarred from entering Welbeck Park and the Birklands.

div.head: Old Order of Camping.
div.p: The Old Order of Camping.

That "the old order changeth "has been forcibly illustrated in the matter of cycle camping, anent the modern developments of which we lately dwelt at length. The passing of the old style of camp is marked by a recent announcement that the Liquidating Committee formed to wind up the Harrogate Camp had held its last meeting, and had discharged all debts. Despite the strenuous efforts of a small band of enthusiasts, that once flourishing annual reunion of cyclists under canvas is now a thing of the past. Although the camp undoubtedly cemented many friendships, and was the scene of sport, conviv ality, and lots of fun, the tendency towards elaborate luxury and liberal hospitality made it a source of heavy expense. Recruits became.scarcer as the years rolled by, the younger men being indisposed to face their share of the cost of furnishing, decorating, /cc., not to mention the aforesaid hospitality. Much the same causes brought to an. end, several years earlier, the series of southern camps which for more than a decade formed a big eature in the cycling calendar. Still, both the old camps were the outcome of unst!nted enthusiasm, honorary labour, and healthy emulation among clubs, while their successful management redounded to the credit of the cycling pastime.

Day is a cycling club fixture regularly catered for by many of the country hostelries patronized by Cyclists.. Where the hotel-keeper is sufficiently enterprising to invest in some special equipment for serving al- fresco refreshments amid the picturesque surroundings of a few score of fairy Umps and Chinese lanterns, these functions are frequently very enjoyable affairs. The period has now arrived when the com- mittees of cyoling clubs venture upon their most ambitious and at,ractive fixtures. With every human likelihood of fair weather, the advocates of a Ladies' Day find their tongues, and garden parties, followed by impromptu dances, commend themselves to many clubs. More expensive to arrange, but highly enjoyable, is the launch trip on the Upper Thames. One club recently held a surprise run, which turned out to be a strawberry tea. Such fixtures, with road handicaps, time trials for medals, and special musters for a club Photograph, diversify the summer list of clhb runs, and do much to strengthen the interest of members in their club. Once introduced into a club, this kind of fixture has a remarkable tendency to repeat itself on every imaginable kind of excuse, and I notice on the fixture card of one London club that ladies are Invited to
The clubs in which the female element is en cou rage d to a reasonable extent are among the Post successful and popular ones.
How Road Records are Made.

lir. G. A. 01ley, whose sensational ride from London to Edinburgh, on a New Hudson bicycle, 'was a notable event of last year, has a capital illustrated article on this subject in C. B. Fry's Magazine' for June. It will be remembered that 011ey rode the 382 miles in 27 hrs. 10 min. over this trying course, beating record. In the article be describes the trial spins, skipping and walking exercise, massage, baths. and food necessary to bring a rider into condition to attempt a similar feat: Very interesting are the details concerning his mount, which weighed 2.21 b., and had wood rims, Constrictor tyres, and a front rim brake. 011ey ran great risks in using these speed tyres for ao long a ride, but he prepared himself for oilier- gency by carrying spare tyres, slipped through the frame and forks, ready for instant substitution if needed. His personal equipment included a mile- age schedule and a watch strapped to his left wrist,

div.head: Doings at Antwerp.
div.p: Doings at Antwerp.
The comparative convenience of Ahtwerp as a continental locale will CIIISC many English people tO visit Belgium for the World's Cycling Chant- bionshins. The entries close on 12th July ”er!.,1,"

Ihtn July the half-yearly meeting ot the Inter- national Cyclists' Association will be held at the Terminus Hotel, close to the central station. The races will take place under the patronage of various 'Belgian royalties, including the King, on what is known as the Zurenborg track. As already men- tioned in this column. the racing dates are the ! Nth, 21st, and 23rd. !Ori the lad day the final of a 5-kilometres motor bicyle championship will take place. Motor pacing will, of course, form a feature in the 100-kilometres championships, and some ! dissatisfaction seems to be felt because the pro- ! meters have imposed no restrictions on the size of ! motors to be used. The American, Walthour, who ! holds the professional title, is reported to have ! intimated his intention of standing down unless he I.acing be restricted to small motors

div.head: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.
div.p: WARRINGTON RURAL DISTRICT COUNCIL.

The monthly meeting of the Warrington Rural Dis- trict Council was heln at Bewsey Chambers on Wednes- day when there were present Mr. Brooks (presiding). Dr. Murray, INTessrs. U. Thompson, J. W. Knowles, Houghton, F. W. Kerfoot (inspector), T. C. Sutton (clerk), B. S. Newcombe (surveyor) and Dr. Sephton (medical ollieer).

div.head: PORT SANITARY AUTHORITY.
div.p: PORT SANITARY AUTHORITY.

The CLERK reed a letter from the Town Clerk of Warrington stating that Councillor Evans had been appointed in place of the Tate Aftlerraau &Mon as joint representative of the Town Council and the Rural District Council on the Manchester Port Sanitary Authority. The appointment was approved. THE NEED FOR A AIORTILTARY AT PEEKETIT.

i The CLERK said he had received a letter- from the Penketh Parish Council stating that they had discussed the question of providing a place in which to put dead bodies while awaiting inquest, and wished the Rural District Council to make arrangements for a place at the Red Lion Hotel to be usediforihe payment of ss. for each body.
Mr. KIsiOWLF.S said the matter was not one for the Rural District Council but purely one for the parish. No action was tahen upon the question. HEALTH OF THE DISTRICT.

Dr. SEPFITON reported that durirm the month there had been 28 births and 21 denths. The death-rate was equal to 221 per 1,000 cc against 361 the average of the last three months and 52.4 for the corresponding period of last year. Exclusive of the eleven deaths which occurred at the Winwick Asylum the denth-rste proper for the district was equal to 108 per 1,000. The health of the district was good.
