div.head: Examiner, Saturday, July 8, 1905.
div.p: The Examiner, Saturday, July 8, 1905.
TRAINING COLLEGE PRIZE DISTRIBUTION.
Canon Morley Stevenson and the
Educational Outlook.
"A GLEAM OF HOPE."

of a teacher. If young people thought they could pass into the profession of a teacher, which was second to none in importance in the country, by any side entrance easily, cheaply, and lightly, they would make a very great mistake, and the country in future would be the poorer because its teachers had not been enriched by all with which the teachers could be enriched within the colleges. (Applause). In the course of an eloquent address, the Rev. Canon KEMPTITORNE congratulated the Principal and tt.e College itself upon the honour the Bishop had coaferred on the Rev. Morley Stevenson in making him a Canon of Liverpool. (Applause.) The Bishop had certainly given honour where honour was due, and he had also expressed his sense of the great importance of the work which Canon Morley Stevenson was doing. He (Canon Kemp- thorne) felt sure that all who cared at all about educa- tion were convinced that the work of our training colleges was quite the most important work from the educational point of view that was going on anywhere in the country. The object of the colleges was to train the minds and eharacters of our future teachers that they in turn might train the minds and characters of the children of England. Their critics sometimes told them that they had different aims in view. It was stated that their aim in such a college as that was to force the minds of young people into con- formity with the views and opinions of the Church of England. The students, however, knew that that was not the aim which the Principal or any of their teachers had in view. They did not want in any of their Church . schools to force the children of Nonconformist parents into conformity with the Church of England. What they claimed was that the children whose parents belonged to the Church of England should be trained in the religion of their parents, and they believed that no other principle was right or just. (Applause.) In the religious teaching given in that college—which formed a small part in point of time, but a very important part in point of influence—the position of the Church of England was plainly set forth. The students knew what the Church taught, but it was not forced upon them. They could test it for themselves by Holy Scripture and in the school of their own exper ence and the teachers were not in the least afraid that if they looked through the thing honestly they would come to know the truth. He did not know whether church people quite realized the debt they owed to training cplleges. The excellence of the teaching in so many of the provided schools was simply due to the fact that the teachers had been thoroughly trained how to teach religious subjects and they had had a splendid I religious influence in the training colleges where they I had learnt their work. (Applause.) If their Church schools were to go—God forbid that they should—if I their Church training colleges were to be dissolved— which he thought would follow the lose of the Church schools—the result would be a general lowering of the tone and standard of religious teaching in all the schools of the country—not only lathe Church sohools but in the provided schools as well. Canon Kempthorne concluded with excellent advice to the teachers. Above all he asked them in their teaching, and especially in religious instruction to be transparently sincere, and never to teach the Children what they themselves did not believe, and if they did not know the answer to a question to admit it,and not pretend to give an answer. (Applause.)

The PRINCIPAL said he had received a perfect shower of telegrams from many people whose absence they very much 'deplored, including the Bishop of Manchester, the Dean of IVlancloester, and Mr. and Mrs. Joynson. He did not think there was anything special in the . history ' of the college during the present year that be ought to touch upon that afternoon. The great:question which bad been in the minds of them all was the matter to which he altu3ed a year ago, and which was now pre- cisely in the same state as it was then—the question of the property of their late neighbours' the Clergy Daughters' School. Most of them would know that the Clergy Daughters' School had removed from Warrington into Derbyshire, and that the property of that school and of the Training College were curiously mixed up in many different ways. It was obviously very essential for the Training College authori- ties that they should have either the property in their own hands or else very charming neigh- bours indeed. (Hear, hear and laughter). How the matter would end, he could not say, but his hoped the negotitations which were pending would result satisfactorily to both parties concerned. With regard to the ;educational outlook generally as it affected Training Colleges' be said last year that whatever the Education Act of 1902 had done, it had certainly stirred i up a great interest throughout the country n the question of education. He thought that was true ; but as well as having stirred up a great interest, it bad also stirred up a great controversy, and they had all, what- ever their private opinions might be, felt sorry for the strain of bitterness and friction which had been raised by the education question throughout the length and I breadth of the land. At the present moment he thought there was a gleam of hope. They had seen in the last few days a very remarkable meeting .in Manchester at which a concordat had been put forth by all parties—a concordat which, if it could be carried outwould—at least that was thb intention of the promoters—bring about educational peace. Whether the concordat was of such a character as to do that which its promoters hoped, he had no intention whatever of expressing any opinion about; but he regarded the very fact that members of the Church of England, Roman Catholics, and Nonconformists could meet together and wish to &well) a concordat, and could agree even to a certain I extent in a certain direction, as a matter of hope for the future. (Hertahear.) On the other hand,some of them had been reading a speech delivered in Liverpool on Friday by one who was certainly a brilliant orator and a clear- headed man and an enthusiast in his cause. He (Canon Stevenson) confessed that when he read the speech he laid it down with a sigh of disappointment and said " Well, these are not the things which make for peace." So they saw on the one hand efforts for agree- ment and on the other hand a great deal of political bitterness which, of course, made the situation much more difficult. \Vhatever the result might be—and they all earnestly hoped that it would be a peace satisfactory to all parties—one thing impressed him very strongly, and that was the very considerable amount of misapprehension and misunderstanding which was rife throughout the country upon the questions con- nected with education. He would like to give them one example which touched the subject of training colleges very intimately indeed. A few yearsago everyone agreed that there was a very urgent demand for greater accom- modation for the training of teachers, but since that time two causes had been in operation which had very much lessened that demand. One was that almost every training college in the country had been enlarged and new training colleges had been built, and the other was that there was a very serious diminution in the number of people who wished to enter training colleges, so that at the present moment, so far from there being a great lack of training college accommoda- tion the amount of accommodation was almost if not exactly equal to the demand which was made upon it. Now for the misrepresentation. Mr. Ackland,—whom they would all remember its minister of education some years ago and he (the speaker) thought one of the best and roost successful ministers who ever sat at Whitehall'— no doubt perfectly unintentionally in a speech which he delivered before the County Councils Association in London represented that there between eleven and twelve thousand students who sat for the entrance examination to training colleges every year and that only between three and four thousand of those could be accommodated in the colleges thus, of course, showing a very serious deficiency indeed in the training college accommodation. The real facts were (to quote the figures for last year) that the number of people who passed the King's Scholarship examination was 11,484, but at that time a pass in the third class did not qualify for admission to as college, so that 5,733 students who passed in that section must be struck off at once. Then 2,133 sat for examination not wishing to enter a college but simply to qualify themselves, so that of the 11,484 who sat and passed no less than 7,866 were either not qualified or not desirous of entei ing n college, and the number of students who were qualified and were desirous of entering was 3,618. div.p: THE PRIZE LIST.
Canon KEMPTII-011—N—E then distributed the prizes as follows

Sinab Carr, Ada Dixon, Ellen Entwistle and Lilian Richards, Divinity ; Emily Taylor, highest marks in all subjects(first prize); Annie Redman,highest marks in all subjects (second prize); Margaret Bidwell, Dora Weston, and Maria Leyland, practical teaching ; Kathleen Arrowsmith and Annie Redman, principles of teaching ; Emily Taylor and Annie Brodie, mathematics ; Sinah Carr, Ada Dixon and Emily Taylor, English literature ; Ellen Elliott, English composition ; Maud Wood, "The best letter" ; Daisy Haywood, Eva Smith and Emily Taylor, reading and recitation ; Annie Redman and Emily Taylor, history and geography ; Emily Johnson, practical science; Ellen Elliott and Emily Taylor, nature study; Emily Johnson and Annie Lidiard, needlework; Alice Barber and Ellen Halsall, drawing (bookwork); Nellie Dale, drawing (black- board); Edith Simpson, theory and practice of music. The Rev. Canon PF.xan vti proposed a vote of thanks to the Rector of Liverpool for distributing the prizes. Mr. R. PIIMPOINT, M.P., seconded and added a lay congratulation to the clerical congratulation already tendered to Canon Morley Stevenson. He was reminded by the fact that Friday was Wall, lug Day and that he was now present at the Training College prize distribu- tion, of a little bit of the history of that school and of the Walking Day, and of how much they owed to those who had gone before them in the times almost forgotten Although that school was not actually founded by the Rev. Horace Powys, still it owed its existence largely to hist initiative about tho year 1839. They all knew that Walking Day was an institution of his, and he (Mr. Piorpoint) conld not help thinking when he saw those thousands of childrenlassemble before the Town Hall what the Rev. Horace Powys would ham thought, could he have seen a day like that.Continning Mr. Pi erpoint agreed with the advice to teachers that if they did not know an answer to a question they should be content to admit that they did not, and in this connection he said he would impress upon the minds of the students one of the wisest sayings of Charles Dickens "Be content to be ignorant of many things in order that you may avoid the unutterable calamity of being ignorant of every- thing." (Applaum). The vote was heartily accorded, and the meeting ended. _ _ .
Tea was afterwards served to the visitors, and the Volunteer Band played an exuallent selection of music on the lawn.
DEATH OF AN OLD FOOTBALLER.

Mr. Ralph Lawson, landlord of the Railway Hotel, Leigh, died on Monday night after three years' illness. Deceased, who was 43 years of age was a native of Aspull, and in the old Rugby Union days was a member of the famous village team, being a county forward. Eighteen years ago he went to Leigh, but retired from football 15 years ago.

div.head: Summ3r Camp.
div.p: Summ3r Camp.

_ Sir,—Arrangements for commencing work at the Camp near Prestatyn, North Wale-s, are now being made. The committee hope to send 10) girls on July 219 t who will return on the '2.3th to be replaced then by another 100. They return on August 4th, when 100 boys will go out who in torn will be replaced by another 100 on August 11th. The committee will be glad to hear of any persons willing to act as °lacers. I have undertaken to act as chief ()Meer during the two weeks when boys will be in camp and T should like to hear from any young men who will act under ma either for one week or two as soon as possible; a postcard will oblige. We are also anxious to send the most needy children and shall be glad to receive suggestions of likely cases from any source. I must also say that the frines required for this work have not come in so far. Souse of those who supported us last year have responded at once to the reminders which have been sent out, but sve shall require the help of all old friends and some who have not given to this object so far, and I trust we shall he well supported by the kVarringtoa public.—Yours truly. ARTHUR 11. LEE, Hon. Treasurer.
Tapestry Works, Brick-street.

div.head: BRIDGE-STREET IMPROVEMENTS. Tradesmen Complain of Loss.
div.p: BRIDGE-STREET IMPROVEMENTS. Tradesmen Complain of Loss.

' Two appeals arising out of the widening of Bridge' street came before the Warrington Assessment Com- mittee at its meeting yesterday (Friday) morning. Mr. AJ. Jolley presided. Mr. T. B. Carter, baker, 22 and f. 14, Bridge-street, applied for a reduction of the assess- ment on his shops amounting to £155 gross and £l3l 10s. ratable. He said the alterations in Bridge- street had involved the taking down of his back premises. including a store-room in which he formerly stored 400 sacks. He had had to utilize another building for storage purposes, and the extra handling entailed when small quantities were required meant a consider- able expense. He estimated his loss in profits during the past six months at £l5O, and altogether he had suffered a loss of £l,OOO through the alterations. Mr. R. Forshaw : I presume the alterations will eventually result beneficially. The Chairman: We are not engaged in prophetic researches. We are dealing with the present. The committee postponed their decision until they had heard an appeal by the Grand Clothing Hall Com- pany against an assessment of £250 gross and £212 10s. ratable. Mr. Ainsworth represented the company and sub- mitted similar reasons to those advanced by Mr. Carter. Owing to the demolition of back property, he had had to take a private house, and Treat inconvenience had been caused to the firm during the busy season. The committee decided to reduce Mr. Carter's assess- ment to £l3O gross and £llO ratable and the Grand Clothing Hall Company's to £2OO gross and £1.70 'ratable. The reduction is temporary, pending the com- pletion of the Bridge-street improvement.

div.head: WEEKLY REPORT ON THE HEALTH
div.p: WEEKLY REPORT ON THE HEALTH
OF WARRINGTON.
WEEK ENDING JULY Ist, 1905.

Daring the week, the following births and deaths were registered:—Warrington Registration District births, 29, deaths, 22. The excess of births over deaths was 7. The birth-rate was equal to 218. The death-rate from all causes was equal to 16.5 per 1,000 against 163 the averai,e o f the previstlS 4 weeks and against TO the corresponding period of last year. The death rate from the seven chief zyrnotic diseases was equal to 3.7 per 1,000, against 24 the average rate of the previous 4 weeks and against 24 the corresponding period of 1901. The ages of mortality were:- 0-1 1-5 5-15 15-25 25-65 65—up. Total 8 4 1 2 5 2 22. The deaths included-3 from measles,2 from diarrhcea, 5 from phthisis, 1 from other tubercular diseases, 3 from lung diseases, 2 from heart disease, 6 from all other causes. The following cases of infectious disease have been reported during Vle week :—Scarlet fever, 2 cases ; puerperal 1 case, phthisis 3 cases. The maximum temperature 81F., was recorded on the 25th June, and the minimum temperature 50F., on the 27th June. The rainfall measured .77inch. The general direction was N.E.

div.head: SAD DROWNING CASE.
div.p: SAD DROWNING CASE.
Warrington Father's Triple Loss,

A painful sensation was created in the Bank Quay neighbourhood on Wednesday evening when the details of a particularly sad drowning case became known. Adjoining the wire works of the Whitecross Company is a large reservoir enclosed by a wall about nine feet high. With the aid of a wire rope attached to a tele- graph post, however, a number of boys scaled the wall. They were, it is supposed, playing on a plank at the side of the reservoir, when John Cawley, aged eight, son of Thomas Cawley, Garahaldi-street, slipped into the water. His com- panions raised an alarm and after the lapse of a short time the body was recovered. Artificial respiration was tried for over an hour, bat unfortunately without effect, and a doctor who was summoned pronounced life to be extinct. A distressing feature of the case is that Mr. Cawley had previously lost two children by burning injuries.

Warrington second team met with no better fate than their colleagues in their match with Liverpool City which was also decided on Tuesday evening. At half- time Liverpool led by two goals to nil, and noon resuming immediately improved their position. War- rington shooting was faulty but Higharn managed to save the team the ignominy of being nilled.

The wmks squadron raoes for the Sir Gilbert Greenell shield were resumed on Tuesday in the Legh-street baths. The holders of the shield (Pearson and Knowles) met the General Post Office (No 2) team and easily accounted for them. A more exciting race was witnessed between Monks Hall and Co. and the Corporation clerks. The clerks were left in the rest after two players had finished but despite this they wiped off a lead of half a length and won by a few yards.

div.head: Cricket.
div.p: Cricket.

The holiday spirit permeated local cricket circles on baturday. and there were very few matches. At Arpley the Warrington first eleven entertained Urmston in a friendly encounter, and a draw was the result. Warring- ton went to the wicket first and the innings realized 137 to which Urmston had responded with 91 for the loss of 7 wickets when the time limit wa.s reached.

There was nothing particularly interesting about the match. Mason, the professional, came out with the top score on the home side, knocking up 36 in really splen- did style. E. Pierpoint and W. Richardson were each responsible for 19, while J. Thompson mtcle 15.

It was rather singular that the highest score for tirruston was also 353 which P. Tyldesley placed to his credit. That player's fine innings practically saved his side from defeat, and he received a full measure of praise for the performance. .
The bowling displays were not particalarlv striking Mends securing the best analysis with 5 SVarrington wicket.; for 60 runs. Mason captured 2 wickets at a :cost of 39.

Among the junior teams, Simkey Wire Mills are haying a highly successful season. The eleven is a capital one, and has not yet suffered a reverse. The other day a pleasant time was spent at Moore, where the president (Mr. E. Houghton) entertainA the players most handsomely.

div.head: Bowling.
div.p: Bowling.

Saturday being Warrington's trip day little bowling was done on local greens fow,if any,orffanized programmes being carried out. To-day play will be resumed and a nurnber of fixtures will be completed. In the Works Competitioi, the second round will be finished the last two matches being between Pearson and Knowles (No. 1) and Cheshire Lines, and Rylands (No. 2) and Fletcher's teams. Pearson and Knowles and Fletcher's should qualify for the third round.

In connection with the Warrington League no league fiAtures are down to be played, the afternoon being devoted to the third of the series of mains which is being held. Play will be over the Fearnhead green and a close game should result.

The main open to the wives and lady friends of the members of the Cemetery Hotel Club will be held on the 20th inst. The question has been raised as to whether the ladies should be handicapped, but as none of the members feel equal to so difficult a task the competitors will probably all start from scratch.
Cycling. Owing to the heavy rain, the Warrington Cyzling Club's run to Chester arranged for last Saturday had to be abandoned.

Tuesday evening was beautifully fine and the roads, after the recent rains, were in gand order. Fifteen members turned out for the visit to Bucklw Hill, which is one of the night fixtures. During the evening several games of bowls were keenly contested.

The members of the club are keen bowling enthusiasts, and about fifty assembled on the Chapel House green on Wednesdny to commence the competition for the silver cup presented by Mr. George Watkins. Owing to the rain, however, only about a dozen games were played. The competition promises to be a great success.

To-day (Saturday) the club will once more be the guest of arr. John Naylor, the esteemed president, at lieeston Towers. Given fine weather, there is sure to be a large muster for the run through picturesque Delamere Forest, while those who prefer to travel by train will take the route via Chester. div.head: Swimming.
div.p: Swimming.

Warrington water polo team cannot exactly be des- scribed as a strong combination. So far this season they have not won a single match and on Tuesd ty they bade good-bye to the "Athletic News" cup. They and their opponents (Everton) were both given byes in the first round of the competition and met in the second round in the Legh-street baths. Last weak they also tried conclusions in connection with the Liverpool and District League and Everton somewhat easily carried off the honours of the game. On Tuesday the Evertonians again triumphed but were set a much harder taskas Warrington did their best to obtain their revenge.

div.head: STOCKTON HEATH AND URBAN POWERS.
div.p: STOCKTON HEATH AND URBAN POWERS.
Time for Action Not Yet Arrived.
THE NEW SCHOOLS,

The question of the advisability of Stockton Heath I seeking to obtain urban powers was!the principal item under discussion at a meeting of the Parish Council which was held on Thursday evening. Mr. Bouchier presided and there were present :—Messrs W. Mclntyre, J. H. Clarke, F. Pearson, J. Hallows, J. Whitley, W. J. ‘Vestbrook and E. Bradshaw (clerk). Mr. Bauchier presented the report of the committee which was appointed to go into the question of the advisability of seeking urban powers. With a popula- tion of 3,500 and a rateable value of £13,000 the parish was called upon to pay annually, poor and county rate, £1,400; expenses of the Rural District Council, £BOO ; and special expenses account LOD, a total of £2,860. Details were given as to the purposes for which the rates were levied and Mr. Boucnier pointed out that while the District Council expenses which were met by Stockton Heath in 1001 totalled only £525, the calls for the present half-year were at the rate of £BOO per annum. In the event of Stockton Heath taking urban I powers the funds at the disposal of such authority would be £1,400 per aanum,—the amount of the District Council and special rates,—out of which would have to j be paid (l) district highways, £310; hospital buildings I account. £34 ; smallpox hospital, £29; disinfection,l £l2; Port S mitary contribution, £9; ship canal opposition, £9; election expenses, £l2; salaries of ofilaers. £6l; establishment charges £46; (2) removal of nightsoil, £110; lighting, £l4O ; sewers sinking fund, £llO ; and officers special allowances £35. (The figures given were the sums expended in the different directions in 1904). The only items in the above which would go towards the cost of administra- tion under an urban council would be :—Salaries of oficers, £Ol ; establishment charges, £46 ; and special allowances to officers, £35 ; a total of £145. Out of that sum would have to he paid the cost of offices and ' the salaries of a clerk, surveyor, and nuisance inspector. ' "At present" continues the report " the parish obtains the services of competent officials at a cost of £145, and your Committee think it would be impossible to obtain equally competent officials and officers exclusively for an urban council at anything like the same figure. , Any extra cost would be a farther burden on the rates.l Another very important matter is the question ,of infectious diseases and small-pox hospitals. Stockton Heath now makes contribution to these , as shown by the above figures. In the event of II our severance from the Runcorn Union, it would be a matter, on adjustment of the figures,as to whether this parish would still be permitted to use these hospitals and on what terms. If we were absolutely cut off for their use we should have to face the cost of erecting and maintaining our own hospitals. To obtain urban powers it would be necessary to apply to the County Council who would hold an inquiry. The cost to Stockton Heath might be anything from £lOO to £l5O according to the nature of the opposition which we should have to meet. The points considered by your committee were (1) the cost of administration under an urban council, towards which there would be ' available from the present rates a sum of £ll5 only, (2) I the cost of an inquiry, (3), the possible refusal of the use of the hospitals Cowards which we now contribute. Oa the other side there are the possible benefits which might result by reason of our having under our control all the affairs of the parish. In this respect Stockton Heath is much better off than it was a few , years ago as administration of the parish affairs is now , more directly under the control of the Parochial Committee. After reviewing the question in all its bearings your committee is unanimously of opinion that the time has not yet arrived when Stockton Heath could with advantage seek urban powers but the parish is growing rapidly and it may be that in the near future the ques- tion might profitably be brought forward for further consideration." Mr. Whitley said that with regard to the small-pox I hospital the Runcorn Urban Council had asked the , District Council for permission for their patients to be received in the hospital upon a consideration. Their request was being considered. Mr. Bouchier : I suppose the question may be arranged beween the two bodies. In our case it would be rather different. If ur sea-Iced ltu th 3 Ramo rra authority it might cause antagonism between them and ourselves and there might be a possibility of their 're- fusing to allow us to use the hospital. Mr. Westbrook explained that at the present time Stockton Heath had a legal right to use the hospital. If they severed themselves from Runcorn would they prejudice that right ? Mr. Whitley : I maintain we shall still have it. Mr. Bradshaw: You will be in the same position as the Runcorn Urban Council. Mr. Hallows: If the Runcorn Urban Council can claim to use the hospital we can. Mr. Westbrook: The Runcorn Urban Cortocil was constituted before the hospital was built. Our Urban Council would no constituted afterwards and no one on earth can say what the terms would be. Mr. Bouchier: Or say whether we would get any terms. Continuing Mr, Bouchier said he did not see that they were in a position to discuss the matter which should go to the parish for consideration. There had been considerable agitation upon the question and a number of people in the parish had thought they should apply for urban powers. The committee had prepared the report for their benefit so that they could see the figures. If any action was taken he thought it should come from outside the Parish C)uncil. He thought the Parish Council were satisfied upon the report, that the time had not arrived when they should apply for urban powers. (lie ar, hear.) The report was adopted.

THE EDUCAMON QUESTION'. Tax POSITION OF YOUNG CRILDREN. Mr. Bouchier reported that the Committee of the Council had met the school managers for the purpose of discussing the proposal of the County Council to erect a new school in the district. They were short of the figures with regard to the number of children going from Stockton Heath to Warrington. They had the number going from Cheshire into the Borough and the Clerk wrote to the director of Education for Warrington to obtain for him the actual number of children going from Stockton 'loath but was informed that it was im- possible to give them. Mr. Bradshaw also tried to get the figures for the County Council and the Rural District Council bat without Success. In tha absence of those figures the committee were unable to consider the matter very fully, and for the purpose of obtaining the figures the meeting was adjourned. It was felt that the matter should be considered not only by Stockton Heath, but also by Walton and Latchford Without, and it was suggested that representatives of the Parish Councils in those two districts should meet the committee of the Stockton Heath Parish Council and the school managers with a view to trying to arrive at some general agreement with regard to that important matter. div.head: GEORGE HOTEL
div.p: THE GEORGE HOTEL
AMOUNT OF COMPENSATION
DECIDED UPON.
Corporation and Tenant's Claims.

.£2,210 is tho amount decided upon as compensation for the licence of the George Hotel, Sankey-street, which the Corporation acquired for street improvement pur- poses. Tao Compensation Authority met on Thursday to assess the amount payable to the Corporation as owners of the licence and Mr. Thomas Halton as tenant of the property. Mr. John Fairclough presided, and the other magistrates on the bench were :—Alderman Bennett, Councillors Wilkinson, and John Roberts, Dr. Fox,Messrs. Charles White,H. Roberts,W. Roberts,R. T. Fairclough, J. Geddes, W. Richardson, If. Thornton, S. Wright, J. W. Hayward, C. Jackson Holmes, and G. Pilling. The magistrates' clerk (Mr, G. F. F. White) said he had advertised the usual notice in the newspapers, and in response he hai received claims for compensation from the Town Clerk and Mr. Thomas Halton. _ . . _ .

The Town Clerk (Mr. J. Lyon Whittle) said he appeared on behalf of the Corporation and the last time he was before the compensation authority heasked for the sum of £3,000. In order to give an idea of the value of the licence, he would put in the valuation of Mr. Thomas Wainwright, who had valued the pro- perty on behalf of the Corporation. The Chairman: Did he value the property or the licence?

The Town Clerk : He valued both together at .25,000. If you take from that the sum of £2,000 for the licence, it gives you £2,000 as the value of the hotel premises. They would not let for anything like £lOO a year,vrnich represents 5 per cent. upon that value. Mr. H. Roberts : Are there any particulars at all to guide us? The Town Clerk handed in Mr. Wainwright's valua- tion. The Chairman: The Corporation have given £13,700 for the whole of the premises, which include the shops of Miss Garner, Mr. Thomas Lee, and Mr. William Parkinson. (To Mr. T. Halton): What was the original rent of the George Hotel ? Mr. Halton : £ll5 a year, which included the shop of Miss Garner. The Town Clerk said that when the Corporation con- templated purchasing the Green Dragon Hotel, Bridge- street, they called in Mr. William Owen, who valued the premises and licence at .21,825. The licence was trans- ferred to the Brooklands Hotel, Lovely-lane. The brewery company expected £l,OOO for the property, and he therefore submitted that the difference between that sum and Mr. Owen's total valuation of £1,821 was the value of the licence. The Chairman: Didn't they give up another licence ? The Town Clerk: No, sir, Continuing, Mr. Whittle said he would remind the Bench that Messrs. Peter \\Talker and Son bad made the substantial offer of £2,550 for the George licence on condition that it was trans- ferred to other premises. The Chairman: The licence may be worth £1 in one ' place and £lOO in another. The Town Clerk: I submit the cases of the George Hotel and the Green Dragon are very similar, as they , are in the same neighbourhood. With regard to Mr. Halton, the tenant, said Mr. Whittle, the Corporation had entered into an agreement with him with regard to the amount of compensation, but at the same time he did not expect the Bench to deal with that now. in the event of the Corporation and tenant not having come to an agreement, the matter would have to be referred to the Inland Revenue Commissioners. Both parties were, however, willing to trust themselves to the Bench. The Chairman :/ Suppose we take an extreme value— say .210—would you divide that sun in the proportion agreed upon between von? The Town Clerk: Yes, we have signed an agreement, but we are prepared to leave the matter in the hands of 1 the Bench. Mr. Henry Roberts thought the proportion to be awarded to the Corporation and tenant respectively was a matter for the Bench to settle. The Magistrates' Clerk : You certainly can say whether you agree or not to what the parties have settled between them. The Town Clerk: You have power to approve of the amount asked for. Mr. Henry Roberts; I think the matter is entirply in our hands. The Town Clerk : Both parties understand that. Mr. H. Roberts : You are no doubt very keen for the interests of the ratepayers, but still you might be disposed to be even more generous than the Bench. Mr. EL T. Fairclough thought the magistrates were in the position of trustees for the public. Therefore they ought to settle the proportion to be awarded to each party. The Bench retired to consider their decision, and on their return into Court the Chairman said they bad approved of compensation to the amount of £2,210 being ~ranted, £7O of that sum to be paid to Mr. Halton. ,

div.head: REDUCING THE VOLUNTEERS.
div.p: REDUCING THE VOLUNTEERS.
Colonel Edelsten and the War Office Proposals.

Consternation has been caused in Volunteer circles by a rececent communication addressed by the War Office to commanding officers. The circular which takes the form of an inquiry, points to the immediate adoption of regulations which will result in the numerical strength of this branch of our auxiliary forces being enormously reduced. Cammanding officers are to see to the personal examination by the medical officers of every man or the roll with a view to preparing a list of those who comply with certain conditions. Those who do not, and the number will not be small, will be classified as unlit for service and will presumably, at a later date, receive their marching orders. In chest, lungs, and heart, volunteers will have to be the acme of perfection; the sliglatest defect in sight or hearing or an imperfection in the arch of the foot will mean expulsion, while the men will have to reach a high state of dental excellence. Moreover, no matter what their physical condition, all men over 45 years of age are to be regarded as" unfit for further service." Finally, when the absurdly strict regulations have been complied with, no man is to be retained unless he is a "first-class shot" according to the conditions of the regulation class. firing. Briefly summed up, the volunteer most be more efficient physically and otherwise than the regular soldier, and as such a thing is practically impossible, it I will naturally mean that a wholesale exodus will be brought about. Colonel Edelsten, the officer command- ing the local volunteer battalion, hesitated to state his opinion on the matter, until the threatened regulations are adopted—if such a drastic step is taken. He, how- ever, thought that the action of the War Office would have an ill effect upon the strength of the battalion as it would make the men disheartened. "It is impos- sible," he said," to expect a volunteer who also has his I private duties to attend to to be as efficient as is regular I soldier, and if the question was put to the House of Commons lam sure the proposals would not be granted."

MEETING OF THE PAROCHIAL COMNIITTEE.

- - -- - The monthly meeting of the Stockton Heath Parochial Committee was held on Thursday evening when there were present:—Nlessrs. J. Ff. Clarke (presiding), W. Nlcintyre, P. Pearson, J. Whitley J. W. Bonchier, J. Fairhurst, H. J. Westbrook, J. Hallows, S. F. Welsby, G. P. Ashton (clerk), J. Swinton (surveyor.) Mr.W. H. J. Jenkins wrote stating that he had met with an accident through the "ridiculous" position in which a lamp post in Mitchell-street was placed. He had had to obtain medical assistance and when be had recovered from the accident he would take steps to make the committee responsible for the damage and expense which he had sustained. Mr. H. J. Westb,mok : Cannot we recover for any possible damage to the lamp post? (Laughter.) It was decided to acknowledge the receipt of the lettar. It was decided to hold future meetings of the committee at the Hall Cafe.

div.head: DEATH OF MR. T BIRCHALL,
div.p: DEATH OF MR. T BIRCHALL,
A Strenuous Career.

Death has removed another of Warrington's most useful and honoured townsmen in the person of Mr. Thomas Birchall, J.P., who passed away at his resi- dence, Holly Lodge, Froghall-lane,last Thursday after- noon. The end was not unexpected, for Mr. Birchall had for some considerable time suffered acutely from asthma and heart trouble, and at his advanced ace— seventy-five—it was felt that the prospect of recovery was very remote. The news of his death was received with the deepest and most widespread regret, for all who had been associated with the deceased gentleman during his long and strenuous career, held him in respect as one who had done his utmost for the welfare of the town.

Mr. Birchall was a Warringtonian, and was always truly proud of the town of his birth. His parents died when he was young, and at the age of fourteen, he was apprenticed to a relative of his mother, Mr. James Edehiten, who carried on the manufacture of iron wire. It was in there early days that he had the good fortune to make the acquaintance of the Rev. Dr. Philip Carpeater, minister at Cairo-street Unitarian Chapel, who exerted a great influence upon him and helped him considerably hi his educational advancement. 'Mr: Birchall persevered in his work and subsequedtly entered the service of the White- cross Co., Ltd. He quickly gained the confidence of the firm and worked his way up to the position of manager which he held for over thirty years. Owing to failing health he relinquished the post a few years ago, but still Continued to take an active interest in the concern.

As a pioneer of the co-operative movement Mr.Biroltall was one of the founders of the Warrington Co-operative Society and the progress of the undertaking was largely due to his untiring exertions. For forty years he held the honoured p isition of president and never missed presiding at a single annual meeting during the whole of that period. He was a firm believer in the advantages of co-opetation to the working classes, and had repeatedly expressed the view that many difficult industrial questions could be solved by a wider application of the principles of co-operation. Mr. Birchall was a staunch Liberal and rendered very valuable assistance to the party in Warrington and district. He was a vice-president of the Liberal Association and had on many occasions addressed public meetings, it being a source of pride to him when expressing his strong faith in the benefits of Free Trade to relate that he had the privilege of hear- ing Cobden speak in the Warrington market place over . sixty years ago. 11 Since 1892 Mr. Birchall had held a seat on the , magisterial bench and was most conscientious in the discharge of the duties. His remarkably regular attendance at the Police Court had earned for him the title of " The Warrington Stipendiary" and he could always be relied upon to devote patient attention to cases, however long and tedious. ' The welfare of the Infirmary and Dispensary was a good cause in which Mr. Birchall had long concerned himself, and for twenty five years he had been ' a member of the Board of Management of the institution. During practically the whole of his life, he had been identified with Cairo street Unitarian chapel, and was honoured and , esteemed by his fellow-members of the congregation. He was generally a speaker at the annual congrega- tional gatherings, and at the last of these meetings which he addressed hp made an earnest appeal to the young people to corns forward and devote themselves to church-work. Mr. Birchall was a sympathser with the P.S.A. movement, and had occasionally figured at , meetings of the Wycliffe Society. To show how sincere was his desire to serve the town, even in his later days, it is only necessary to state that Mr. Birchall acted as a Commissioner at the recent inquiry into the trading transactions of the Corporation, and was a regular attender at the sittings. Of a kindly and pleasant disposition, Mr. Birchall commanded a large circle of. friends, and his death ' creates a gap which it will indeed be difficult to till. He leaves a widow, a son, and three daughters, with whom much sympathy has been expressed in their bereavement.

div.head: FUNERAL.
div.p: THE FUNERAL.

Striking evidence of the respect in which the late Mr. Birchall was held was forthcoming at the funeral which took • place at the Warrington Cemetery on Monday morning. The large and representative attendance testified to the active part which the deceased gentle- man played in the life of the town and the deep regret occasioned by his death. The first part of the service was conducted in Cairo-street chapel where the cortege was joined by the members of the Corporation and others. The Rev. W. H. Drummond, a former minister of the chapel, and the Rev. C. Harvey Cook officiated, The hymn "Nearer my God to Thee" was feelingly sung Mr. J. M. Muir presiding at the organ. In the course of a short address the Rev. W. H, Drummond said: We stand this morning in the , presence of death, and howsoever and at whatsoever time death comes to men it is always a deep mystery. Sometimes it comes to the opening life, and the first promise of beauty is cut off. Sometimes it comes in the middle of our days when the heart is still eager and the frame still active, and sometimes it-comes when the day is far spent, when life's work is done, and the old man lies down to take his rest. But, as we stand in the presence of death, let us remember that we stand also in the presence of God, who is the vanquisher of death, and when the heart needs Him most then He is al ways most near. Our thought of death, as Christian people, is for ever linked with the thought of Jesus Christ, of His ministry of compassion, His gracious promises, and His own victory over the powers of the grave. And it is in this spirit of Christian faith that we , would say "farewell" to the earthly presence of our aged friend and commit him into the Divine keeping in whom he trusted. As this is no time for judgment. so it is no time for praise. Still, I think, as we are gathered together, we maw venture to express our thankfulness for whatever has been faithful and good, for everything that has made for the happiness and the welfare of his fellow-townsmen. Your presence here shows that you feel that his career amongst you has been a very useful one, that he has fulfilled the difficult duties of citizen- , ship worthily, that he has been faithful to the many causes of human progress and enlightenment to which many years ago he first set his hand. The public life of your town will be the poorer without him,and this place in which we are now gathered, in which for many long years he worshipped God, will long miss his t familiar presence and his devoted interest in its welfare. And so we commit him to the divine keeping in the faith of our Saviour Christ, as he passes into the nearer , presence of God and life everlasting. I At the close of the service the organist played " 0 rest in the Lord." A procession was formed, headed by members,, of the Police Force in charge of Chief Inspector Phillips, and proceeded to the Cemetery. The last rites at the graveside were performed by the Rev. W. 11. Drummond. The chief mourners were :—Mrs. Robert Pemberton and Miss Birchall(daughters), Mr. C. A. Pemberton and Mr. Robert Pemberton (grandsons) ; the Rev. J. H. Bibby (Bailee), Mr. W. W. Yates (Dews- bury), Mr. William Gill, Mr. W. Furness and Mr. C. H. Johnstone. The Cairo-street Chapel and Sunday school were represented by Mr. J. W. Davies (secretary) and Mr. F. W. Purse (treasures) ; the Co-operative Society by Messrs. A. H. Rathbone (managiug secretary), W. I Ford (cashier), and the following members of the com- mittee :—Messrs. Dimbobhin, W. Jeffrey, E. Williams, T. Critchley, F. Tim perley, Henry Maybury, and Edward Malone. The St. lielens Co-opera- tive Society was represented by Mr. Joseph Elllison (chairman), Mr. J. H. Winterbottarn (manager) ; the Brymbo Society by Mr. C. S. Hughes ; the Runcorn Society by Mr. W.W. Millington (president), Mr. W. M. Morris (menager), anti Mr. J. J. I ' Shaw (secretary), and the Co-operative Union by Mr.! W. E. Dudley. The following members of the Cor- poration and officials were also present :—Aldermen Fairclough (deputy Mayor), Bennett and Tinnion. Councillors Brough, Wright, Ellison, Sankey, and Skelland ; Mr.T. Longdin (borough surveyor), Mr.W.H. Woodcock (representing the borough treasurer and staff), Mr. T. H. Spinks (chief clerk in the Town Clerk's department), Dr. J. Guest Gornall (medical officer of health), Mr. Charles Madeleyl (librarian and I curator(, Mr. F. Taylor (secretary of the gas depart- ment), and Mr. F. O. Ruddock (analyst). The magis- trates in attendance, in addition to members of the Council, were Messrs. F. Monks, Zilsa Armitage, John I Fairclough, Charles White, R. T. Faircicugh, A. J. ' Jolley, J. Rymer Young, H. Roberts, W. Roberts. H. Thornton, S. Wright, arid J. W. Hayward. The White. cross Co., Limited was represented by Messrs. Walter Milner (a director), J.W. Bouchier,A.Walsh, R.Wribster, I J. Owen ; the Board of Management of the Infirmary by j the Revs. John Yonge (chairman) and W. Bracecamp end Messrs. John Fairclough, F. Monks, C. White H Thornton, and J. H. J. Harupson (secretary), and the Liberal Association by Alderman Tinnion and Mr. J. Owen. Amongst others present were the Rev. Canon Morley Stevenson, the Rev. J. F. Matthews, and Messrs. William Long, J. A. Young, S. Davies, Arthur Browne, Thomas Birtles, Andrew Rathbone, William Winstanley, John Houghton, George Wallington, Isaac Mills, P. L. Richardson, J. E. Richardson, T. S. Steel, J. H. Knowles, T. Whittle, W. Bennett, Leonard Bennett, N. Cook, J. Haley and W. Jones. The following acted as bearers :—Messrs. John Johnson, E. Starkey, W. Kay, Banner, Critchley and Albinson (representing the Co- operative Society). Mr. C. Jackson Holmes nad written to say that he regretted to be unable to attend the funeral owing to absence Irons Warrington. The funeral arrangements were carried out by Mr. George Wallington. There were no flowers by request, but two wreaths from the family were placed on the coffin. PUBLIC REFERENCES.
MAGUTERIAL.
Before the commencement of the ordinary business at the Police Court on Saturday, Mr. J. W. Hayward, who

presided, referred to the great loss the Bench had sus- tained by the death of Mr. Thomas Birchall, who was for a number of years chairman of thst Court on Satur- day mornings. He was very well known and highly esteemed by all his colleagues, and discharged his =Os' terial duties and other responsibilities with the greatest, interest and fidelity, and they deeply mourned his loss. He took a great interest not only in the work of the court, but in those who appeared in it, and to his (the speaker's)knowledge he had followed the people who had been brought before him, and sought to bring about their betterment. Mr. R. T. Fairclough said he felt very sorry when he heard of the death of Mr. Birchall. He had taken a great interest in the work of that court, and the people who had been brought before him. He used to follow up many cases, and had done a large amout of good outside the work of the court.

Dr. Fox also referred in fitting terms to the loss which the Bench had sustained,; Alderman Bennett said he would like to add his tribute to Mr. Birchall. As a younger magistrate, he ha l not had the experience in court which some of thera had with Mr. Birchall, but, as a townsman, he appre- ciated his strenuous services. He did not think in the. whole of Warrington there was any citizen more devotedly attached to the town, and more anxious to serve the various spheres which had opened up ,such: as the Co-operative Society, the lufirmary,and, latterly, the faithful service he had rendered as a commissioner in the Non-trading Inquiry. It was only right that they should convey their sympathy to the relatives. Mr. H. Thornton said he fully endorsed all that had been said about Mr. Birchall. He was a very pleasant man to work with, and as consistent as it was possible, to be. Re felt like the other magistrates that the deepest sympathy should be conveyed to the widow and family. The Magistrates' Clerk (Hr. G. F. F. White) said he associated himself with the remarks which had been made, and he would convey the expressions of sympathY to the widow and family. Ur. Taylor (Police Court Missionary) said he would also like to add his tribute to Mr. Birchall's worth. He could personally testify to the deep interest Mr. Birchall had taken in the work of the court. He had paid many visits to the Liverpool Home and the local }braes, and his loss would be keenly felt. LATCHFORD BAPTIST CHAPEL. The Rev. J. F. Matthews referred to the late Mr. r. Birchall in his address at the Latchford Baptist Church on Sunday evening. He said it was not his habit from that pulpit to refer to all the public men who passed away in Warrington. He could not refrain, however, from mentioning the very recent decease of their friend, Thomas Birchall. He had been in the best sense a popular man. His marked integrity, his hatred of all shams and cant, his plain, direct speech, were united with a saintliness of character which compelled the respect of all his fellow citizens ; while those who came to know him more intimately conceived a warm. affection for him. Such a man helped to keep alive and foster the highest purity in public life. Theologically he was a Unitarian, with a nature devoutly religious, and withal a man of broad synarithies. Warrington public life was the poorer for his death, the richer,how- ever,for the influence and example of his life while here, and gracious memories would always be associated with his name.

div.head: DEATH OF THE REV. RICHARD GREENALL.
div.p: DEATH OF THE REV. RICHARD GREENALL.

CAIRO-STREET CHAPEL. The Rev. W. H. Drummond, of All Saints' Church. Belfast, conducted the service in Cairo-street Chapel 013 Sunday morning. At the close of his address he spoke of Mr. Birchall's long connection with the chapel and schools. " Mr. Birchen, he said," was faithful in hiS attachment to this place. He loved its traditions. He loved the simple message of divine love and Christian discipleship which he heard within its walls. Hie memory often lingered round his own early recollec- tions, and especially round the figure of the venerated teacher of his own boyhood, whose name was often on his lips. Succeeding ministers have found in him staunch and kindly friend, who never failed in his interest in their work. It is not too much to say—he would have been the first to acknowledge it—that it was here that he found the inspiration for the discharge of public duty and for every honourable position of nsefulne which he has been called upon to fill. I think we shells all feel how fitting are the words. whenapplied to him, ; " Lord, I love the habitation of Thy house, and thin place where Thy glory dwelletb." REI'F,RENCES AT THE TOWN COUNCIL MEETING. MR. BIRCIIALL'S SERVICES AS AN INQUIRY COMMISSIONER. At the meeting of the Warrington Town Council, on' Tuesday evening, the Mayor, who presided, said that I was with much regret that he had to remind the Council I. of the death of Mr. Thomas Birchall. The town . • lost a good and useful citizen. While it was not us for the Council to express its condolence on the deat, )f persons who had not been connected with the cor, porate body, he thought that having regard to t. eminent public services rendered to the town by 311 Birchall as a magistrate, and, bearing in mind the 10, and very useful services he had recently given to the , Council in the arduous and painful inquiry, he (the speaker) felt bound to propose to them that o°l express their deep regret at the loss the town had sus- tained by the death of Mr. Birchen, and to express their sympathy with his widow and family in their sad bereavement. He would, therefore, propose a resolution in the words he had expressed. (Hear, hear.) Alderman Bennett seconded. fie could echo every word the Mayor had said with reference to the services rendered by Mr. Birchen to his native town. Warring- ton did not possess a more honourable and upright citizen, nor one who, in his own way, and on his own lines, was more anxious to serve the town. His servieeS' were varied in nature, and covered many fields, and, although he had never served in the Council, theF would remember the strenuous and valuable service he rendered them in the crisis through which they receotl9 passed in connection with the inquiry. He (Alderival, Bennett) had the honour of proposing the deceaseo gentleman as one of the memernbers of that commission, and the selection was abundantly justified by the ser" vices he rendered. The faithful, diligent, and assiduous attention which he gave to that work was reflected le all his public work. They could not too sincere ly express the loss theyliad sustained by his death. (Hear,

hear). Councillor Evans endorsed what the Mayor and Alderman Bennett had SAN. He had known 3lr* Birchall for a long time, and Warrington would be the poorer for his decease. (Hear, hear). The resolution was unanimously carried.

. ~..y our readers, that we arm:mince the death of the lie Richard Greenall, rector of Grappenhall, who passed away at six o'clock on Wednesday morning at ll'e Rectory, (frappentiall. The deceaso,u. clergyman was a son of the late Sir. Thomas Greenali, of Wildersp)ol, and received his early education at the Liverpool Institute under Conybeare and Howson - From thence lie went to Brazenose College, Oxford.* where he took his B.A. degree in 1852. During 1114 term at college he was a most enthusiastic oarsmau and acted as president of the University Boat He was was the possessor of several cup's and meda'' gained in notable races, and he had rowed in the college boat in Oxford and Cambridge contests, He also assisted Oxford when they won the grand challenge cup, the stewards' plate, and t" Ladies' plate at Henley. Mr. Greenall was ordainedf deacon in 1853 and priest in 1854 by the Bishop . Eceleston, St. Helens, but left the district in 1830 to become curate, in charge of Christ Churcb* Latchford. He then becanl° vicar of Stockton Heath and during the six years 11 had charge of the work there, gained the respect n't( esteem of his parishioners. In 1881 he removed. tr' Devonshire and lived in retirement until 1890 when he accepted the living of Stockleigh-English in the diocesre. of Exeter. Mr. T. W. H. Crosland, the author of " Lovely Woman " and a few libal actions, has returned to the field of literature. This week he discourses on parentage in the following characteristically caustic manner :—" The state of parentage is a state of vanity. If there is anything vainer than a father, it is a mother. Too many children are encouraged to fiddle, and draw, and paint, and squawk, and scribble and read for this, that, or the other, simply because their parents are sand-blind with vanity." * * An innovation hit upon by the Warrington Educa- tional authorities has met with a mixed reception, depending, of course, upon th 3 point of view of the people concerned. The students, who attended the evening classes at the Technical Institute last session were not aware that a "recording angel " was minutely chronicling their doings for future reference. Last week-end, however, they received post-cards coldly setting forth such interesting particulars as :-:Number of times absent; percentage of marks awarded for home lessons and test examinations ; order of merit; general comments. It is not always pletsant to be reminded ot such facts - especially at holiday times—and we are afraid some students are inclined to regard the departure as misdirected energy. Parents, however, view the matter inn different light, ani there will probably have been some unexpected reckonings with wayward students.
